01.1: Welcome. Today is Session 1, and the question for the next two hours is which work suits AI, which suits ordinary software, and which stays with professional judgement. I will not start with slides. I start with a few spoken questions so I can hear how you think about AI now. Everything we use today is fictional: the firm, the clients and the contract.
01.2:
Before I explain anything, I ask the entry questions orally, one at a time, and I write down your reasons as well as your answers. There are seven, and this slide holds the first one. I leave the earlier result off the screen so you are not guided.

I ask: name one task you trust AI with today, and one task where you would always check its output. Tell me why for each.

Any concrete example is fine. The reason is what I record, because it is our baseline. If you say "I trust it to tidy an email, but I check anything with a figure in it", that already tells me where your line sits. By the end of today we want one candidate task from your own firm, so I listen for tasks that could become that.

Now I show you the matter we will use all day.
01.3:
This is the matter. Kampala Legal and Tax acts for Victoria Services Ltd, the customer and our client. Its service provider is Equator Systems Ltd. Equator has told Victoria it proposes an internal reorganisation, and Victoria wants to know whether the agreement requires its consent. We do not yet know who owns what after the reorganisation, or whether Equator stays responsible. Everything here is fictional.

I ask: if this landed on your desk this morning, what would you ask for first?

A good answer names the signed agreement, the facts of the proposed transaction, the client's instruction, and any records the advice depends on. If you start with "what does the law say", I ask what the agreement itself says, because the contract is the first source.

Next is the set of documents we will keep returning to.
01.4:
This is the folder we work from. It holds four kinds of material. First, the executed agreement, CONTRACT-01 v2. Second, the older draft v1, the firm playbook and the client's instruction. Third, the financial records: sales, credit notes, ledger and receipts. Fourth, public sources such as legislation, judgments and URA guidance.

An AI tool could read all of these in seconds. That does not make them equal. The executed agreement is evidence of what the parties agreed. The superseded draft v1 is history. The playbook is the firm's own policy. A judgment is public authority.

I ask: if the draft and the executed agreement disagree, which one answers the client's question, and why?

You should say the executed version, because it is the one that binds the parties. A partial answer, such as "the newest one", deserves a follow-up: how do you know which is newest?

Now we put a name on what these tools are.
01.5:
Here is a working definition of an AI system. It is a system that takes inputs and infers how to produce predictions, content, recommendations or decisions for a goal. The phrase to hold on to is "infers". A filing cabinet stores a record and gives it back unchanged. An AI system works out an output from what you give it. Systems also differ in autonomy and adaptation. The lower line adds that AI is also the field of study that builds such systems.

This is a paraphrase of a published definition, and it says nothing about how well any product performs.

I ask: if a vendor says its product meets this definition, have you learned that it is reliable?

The answer is no. The definition says what kind of thing it is. Reliability comes from testing it on your task. If you answer yes, I ask what test you would run on a firm task.

Next we separate the labels people mix up.
01.6:
This table sorts four terms by what the work is. Data analysis means examining data to answer a question, such as reconciling sales and receipts. That can be done in a spreadsheet with no AI at all. Data science is the wider practice of using computing, statistics and subject knowledge to study data. Machine learning means a program learns patterns from examples, such as predicting which category a document belongs to. Deep learning is machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. A neural network is a program built from layers of small connected calculations.

I ask: take an invoice total of 4,820,000 shillings across twelve lines. Would a language model do that addition better than a calculator?

The answer is no. Exact arithmetic has a defined right answer, so a calculation tool should do it. The AI can help prepare the data or explain the result. If you say yes, I ask how you would check the model's total.

Now to the kind of AI most people have met.
01.7:
Generative AI is a kind of AI model that produces new content, such as text, by modelling patterns it learned from data. A model here is the trained program itself. In our matter the task is to draft a response using the client's instruction and the approved clause.

The draft will read well. Wording that is new can still contain a claim the contract does not support, because the model produces likely text and does not look up a fact. So the draft is a proposal to check against the source.

I ask: Victoria's draft reply reads smoothly and sounds confident. What does that tell you about whether it is correct?

The satisfactory answer is that it tells you nothing about correctness. You check each factual claim against the agreement. If you say a confident tone is a good sign, I ask you to recall a human colleague who sounded sure and was wrong.

Next I draw how these fields sit inside one another.
01.8:
This slide builds in five clicks, and I stop after each one. The first click shows the largest field, artificial intelligence. The second adds machine learning inside it, the part where programs learn patterns from examples. The third adds deep learning inside machine learning. The fourth adds generative AI, which describes the ability to create content and often uses deep learning. The fifth adds the side notes: data science overlaps all of these and also includes work with no machine learning, and natural language processing, or NLP, is the study of how computers handle human language.

I ask: is every data analysis task a generative AI task?

A satisfactory answer says no. Counting records, sorting documents into categories and drafting a letter are three different jobs. If you say yes, I ask which of those three a spreadsheet already does.

Now I turn these ideas into the actual tasks in our matter.
01.9:
Here the ideas become tasks. Totalling invoice amounts is calculation and gives a number. Identifying a contract type is classification and gives a category. Finding a precedent clause is retrieval, which means searching a collection and returning the passages it found. Drafting an amendment is generation and gives proposed wording. Each task has its own test of success: the number is right, the category is right, the passage is relevant and current, the wording is accurate and fit for purpose. One workflow can mix several of these.

When people say "AI" they often mean a single chat tool, so this table is how I show that one name covers different jobs.

I ask: of these four, which output would you never send out without a lawyer's decision?

Every output needs a use decision, and the amendment needs a partner's review most of all. If your answer is only "the draft", I ask what decision applies to the number.

Next I show where the model sits in a working tool.
01.10:
This slide builds in four clicks. The first click shows the person, who brings the question and the authority to ask it. The second shows the application, which holds the files and instructions. The third shows the model and its tools, where the generating or searching happens. The fourth shows review, where a person decides how the output may be used.

Take our question about the agreement. A model that has not been given the executed agreement cannot tell us what it says. A tool can fetch the document, and a person still checks what came back. An API is a way for one program to ask another to do something, and it is how such pieces often connect.

I ask: where in this chain should the check on who may see a restricted document happen?

A good answer puts it before the system returns the evidence or takes an action. If you say at the review step, I ask what has already been exposed by then.

Next, a simpler contrast.
01.11:
Two approaches sit side by side here. A rule follows logic someone wrote down: when a recorded review date arrives, send a reminder. A learned prediction is a model's estimate based on examples, such as which incoming documents belong to a matter. The estimate can be wrong on a new document, and the rule does not guess. Both can live in the same firm.

I ask: a limitation period date is already on the file. Which approach do you use for the reminder, and who owns the date?

The satisfactory answer is a maintained date field with a simple rule, and a named person responsible for the date being right. A rule only works if the date is correct. If you pick the model, I ask what you would show it as examples, and whether you would trust it on a date that has legal effect.

Now we put a real question to the contract.
01.12:
Now the first contract question. Victoria asks whether the agreement requires its consent for the transaction. The answer sits in Section 12.6, and the version that governs is the replacement in the Key Terms. The Key Terms override the Section 12.6 in the Standard Terms. I read the replacement aloud in full. Neither party may assign without the other's prior written consent. Provider must get Customer's prior written consent before a change of control of Provider takes effect. That consent is not required for a reorganisation within a wholly owned group if Provider remains responsible for its obligations.

I ask: can we answer yes or no right now?

We cannot. The exception has two conditions, and we do not have the ownership chart or any confirmation that Equator remains responsible. If you say "it is internal, so no consent", I ask how we know the group is wholly owned.

Now I show two ways an AI answer could read.
01.13:
Here are two answers to the consent question. The first reads: every change of control requires prior written consent. It is fluent and short, and it leaves out the exception. The second says prior consent applies to a change of control, and a reorganisation inside a wholly owned group is exempt if the provider remains responsible. I hold the Key Terms text of Section 12.6 beside them and have you find the missing words.

I ask: what makes the second answer more useful to the partner?

A good answer says it keeps the condition and can be traced to the source. It still depends on the facts, which we do not yet have.

If the connected tool is available, this is where we put the real question to it and keep whatever it returns, right or wrong. If it is unavailable, I use the labelled example and mark that step as not run.

Next, a boundary on what we may feed these tools.
01.14:
Before you use any tool with this material, we set a boundary. In class, public authorities and our fictional client records are fine. Real client material is different. It needs a permitted tool, a stated purpose and an access decision. Confidentiality and personal data duties apply, and some matters are restricted. A personal subscription does not by itself give a firm the right to upload client files. I keep this short today, and Session 11 covers governance in detail.

I ask: in your firm, who decides whether a real matter may go into a tool?

A satisfactory answer names the person designated to own the information, and an approver under the firm's duties. If you say "whoever is using it", I ask who answers to the client if something leaks.

Now we pick a task to work on.
01.15:
This table offers three candidate tasks. Precedent search aims to find relevant firm knowledge, and its first constraint is current sources and permissions. Contract comparison aims to find departures from the playbook, and it must preserve qualifications such as the exception we just read. Tax evidence review aims to find discrepancies between records, and it needs complete and comparable records.

You choose one, and we record it as a hypothesis to test later. I do not ask for a promised saving. We come back to this choice after the data and risk sessions.

I ask: which one could your firm investigate first, and what would a good result look like?

A strong answer picks a narrow task with evidence you can reach and a way to tell whether the output is right. If you pick something broad, I ask which single document type you would start with.

Now we do the work in class.
01.16:
This is our in-class work, and we do it together. I run it in four steps. First we discuss how you use AI today, using the answers I recorded. Second, you ask the assistant the clause question with the evidence you choose. I demonstrate once so you see the steps, and then you choose the evidence for a changed version of the question. Third, we compare the response with the complete clause. Fourth, you pick one firm task and a success test.

This needs a connected account, so I rehearse it in the real account before class. If the tool is unavailable, I use the labelled example, mark that step as not run, and keep time for the explanation. I save the actual output either way.

I ask: before you press enter, what do you expect the answer to include?

Then we look at what we can conclude.
01.17:
Now we say what today's work shows. Calculation, learned classification, retrieval and drafting are different operations. The base facts do not establish every condition of the exception. A pilot needs an owner, permitted evidence and a test for the specific task. The second point is a limit: one opening demonstration and an entry diagnostic say nothing about how a tool performs in production.

I ask you to say the conclusion in your own words first, and then I compare it with this slide.

I ask: which part of today's result is still unverified?

A good answer says that one run shows what happened once and does not show how often the tool is right. If you only repeat the first point, I ask what you would need to see across many documents before relying on it.

Next we record the decision.
01.18:
We record one decision. Select one task to investigate, and write down how it is done today, who owns the source material, and what is still uncertain. Then note the evidence you still need. This is a decision record for our class and does not authorise anything in your firm.

I write down a proposed owner and one condition with you before we move on. For the contract comparison task, an owner might be the partner who maintains the playbook, and a condition might be that only fictional or permitted documents are used.

I ask: what evidence would change this proposed decision?

A satisfactory answer is that you would revisit it if the quality results, the source material or the permitted scope changed. If you say nothing would change it, I ask what result you would accept as a reason to stop.

Last, a short check.
01.19:
This is the check, and I ask all three before showing any answers. I ask: a deadline is fixed and a reminder is needed, would you train a model? Then: a draft quotes the contract but leaves out the exception, is it usable? Then: name one person who owns the source material for your chosen task.

A good set of answers goes like this. For the date, keep a maintained date and a simple rule. The draft fails on completeness because it left out the operative exception, so it is not usable as it stands. For the owner, name the real or proposed person who looks after that matter's sources.

If one answer is partial, I change the facts and ask again: what if the date were uncertain, who would you ask?

That is Session 1. Next time, Session 2, we look at how AI learns and represents information.
01.20:
This is an optional slide. I use it only if you ask what a model is or we have spare time. A model is a mathematical representation that maps inputs to outputs. Its structure or settings can be written by hand or learned from data. Those settings are called parameters. In our matter, the model is one part inside the application you see on screen.

I ask: does the chat window you type into describe the whole AI system?

A good answer says no. Files, search, tools, permissions and logs can all sit around the model. If you say yes, I ask where the agreement you uploaded is kept.

Then I return to the closing check.
01.21:
This is an optional slide for when you want to look at how things go wrong. Each line is a different stage with a different error. An extraction can lose a word, such as the word "wholly". A search can fetch an old version of a document. A draft can state a proposition the source does not contain. An action can send something to the wrong person.

Reliability comes from tests that fit each task, and I avoid any claim that one tool is always accurate.

I ask: a search returns the superseded draft v1 instead of the executed agreement. Would rewording the question fix it?

The satisfactory answer is no. The sources and the search process need to change. If you say yes, I ask what the reworded question would do to the version list.

Then we go back to the closing check.
01.22:
This optional slide gives our working definition of an AI-native firm for this course. It is mine for teaching and is no formal standard. Work is designed to use AI where evidence supports it. People keep defined responsibilities and authority to review. The firm maintains usable information and measures outcomes.

I ask: what would a firm have to change before a knowledge assistant could be useful?

A good answer names source ownership, matter access, version control and an agreed review procedure. Not every task should use AI, and the point is that the firm can show where it helps. If you answer with a product name, I ask who keeps its documents current.

02.1:
Welcome back. Last session we separated what an assistant calculates from what it writes. Today we look inside one step further. We cover how a model learns from examples, and how a sentence from a contract becomes numbers a computer can compare. We use the same matter throughout, Victoria Services Ltd and its agreement with Equator Systems Ltd. I ask for no maths. I ask for clear questions you could put to a vendor.

The next slide opens with a recall question from Session 1.
02.2:
I ask the recall question before I say anything about the answer. I read it aloud: "An assistant totals invoices and drafts a letter. Which operation needs learned generation?" Then I stay quiet and let you think.

I am listening for the letter. The total should come from defined arithmetic, the same sum every time. If you say both need the model, I ask: "If the invoices add up to a different figure on a second run, would you sign the ledger?" That brings the answer out.

Then I read today's question from the slide and the result line: an explanation of training, inference, tokens and similarity using the same matter.

Now I start with the model itself, and the third slide sets out the tasks we will keep in view.
02.3:
Here I define the term we will use all session. A large language model is a computer program built from a neural network. A neural network is a set of connected calculations, each controlled by numbers called parameters. The model was trained on a very large amount of text, and it works by predicting which token comes next. A token is a small piece of text, often a word or part of a word. I will say more on tokens shortly.

Then I point at the second box. Classifying an agreement, pulling out a party name and writing a clause are three different jobs.

I ask: "If a vendor says its tool is accurate, which of those three jobs do you ask about first?" A good answer names the job and asks how it was tested on documents like ours. If the answer is vague, I ask what a wrong result would cost the firm in that job.

Training comes next, because every claim about accuracy depends on it.
02.4:
Training means fitting a model to data. The model starts with parameters set to rough values. We show it examples, and the parameters are adjusted so its answers get closer to a target we chose. That target is the objective.

Take the box on the slide. The firm labels a pile of past documents as agreements or invoices. A classifier looks at them and adjusts itself until its labels match ours. 

I ask: "When we say the model was trained, what exactly was changed?" I am listening for the parameters, the internal numbers, and that the change came from the examples and the objective. If you say it learned the facts, I ask: "Where would those facts be stored, and can we point to them?" That shows you that the parameters hold patterns and not a list of documents.

The next slide shows the loop that does this adjusting, one step at a time.
02.5:
This slide has four clicks. Each one adds a stage of the loop.

The first click shows Examples, the inputs with their targets: a document and its label. The second shows Prediction, the model's current output for an example. The third shows Comparison, the gap between prediction and target, and the fourth shows Update, where the parameters move a little to shrink it. Then the loop repeats over many examples.

After the fourth click I read the line at the bottom: evaluate on relevant unseen data rather than training fit alone. A model can shrink its error on the examples it has seen by memorising them.

I ask: "A vendor shows you a chart where the error falls steadily during training. What else do you need before you trust it?" What I want to hear is results on documents the model never saw, of the kind we handle. If you stop at the chart, I ask: "Would the chart look the same if the model had simply memorised the examples?"

Different kinds of feedback drive this loop, and the next slide names four.
02.6:
This table names four ways a model can get its feedback. I take them one row at a time.

Supervised means we supply the target label, such as telling the model each document is an agreement or an invoice. Unsupervised means there are no labels for the task, and the model looks for structure, for instance groups of similar documents. Self-supervised means the targets come from the data itself. That is how language models learn from plain text. Reinforcement means the model receives a reward from interaction and improves its choices of action.

I ask: "You have ten thousand old letters and nobody has labelled them. Which approach could you start with, and what would it give you?" A good answer says unsupervised, and that it would offer groups of similar letters to inspect, and the groups still need a person to read them. If you pick supervised, I ask who would supply the labels and how long that would take.

Whichever approach we use, we need to keep some documents aside, and that is the next slide.
02.7:
A model is only as trustworthy as the test we give it, so we split our documents into three sets. I read the three boxes.

Training examples fit the parameters. Validation examples help us choose settings, like how long to train. The held-out test checks the final choice on documents the model has never seen, and we use it once at the end.

Here is the legal wrinkle. Suppose near-identical copies of one service agreement land in both training and test. The model looks excellent because it has effectively seen the answer, so we split by matter or document family. 

I ask: "Why would you take a near-duplicate of a training document out of the test set?" I am listening for the point that the test would then measure familiarity and not performance on new work. If you say it wastes space, I ask: "If the test is easy because the model has seen it, what does a good score tell you about next month's new matters?"

Having covered how a model is trained and tested, the next slide shows what a neural network does inside.
02.8:
This slide has four clicks, and each adds a part of a small illustrative classifier.

The first click shows Inputs, the document features, which are numbers describing a document, such as how often certain words appear. The second shows Layer 1, which mixes those features into learned combinations. The third shows Layer 2, which mixes those combinations again. The fourth shows the Output, a type score, for example how strongly the document looks like an agreement. 

When there are several layers, each building on the one before, we call it deep learning. The slide says it is not a biological brain. It is arithmetic done many times.

I ask: "In this picture, which numbers were learned in training, and which number comes in fresh today?" What I want to hear is that the connections are learned parameters and the document features are today's input. If the answer mixes them up, I ask: "If we feed in a different document tomorrow, which part of the picture changes?"

Now we turn to how text enters a model, starting with the token.
02.9:
A model cannot read letters the way we do. It first cuts the text into pieces called tokens. A token can be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark, or for images a patch. The slide says tokenisation depends on the model, which means two models can cut the same sentence differently.

The box on the slide gives the point for our work. A common word like "agreement" may be a single token. A rarer legal word such as "indemnification" may be split into several pieces. Each piece is then given a number, an ID, which only names the piece.

I ask: "Does one token always equal one word?" A good answer says no, it depends on the tokenizer and on the text. If you say yes, I ask: "How would a model cut the word 'indemnification', and who decides?"

A token only names a piece of text. The next slide covers the numbers that carry meaning, called embeddings.
02.10:
An embedding is a list of numbers that represents an item, such as a word, a sentence or a whole clause. The numbers are built so that we can compare items by computer. Two passages whose lists are close under our chosen measure are treated as related.

Our box gives the use. We have a query about group restructuring, and we have candidate passages from the contract. A system turns the query and each passage into lists of numbers using the same embedding model. It then ranks the passages by how close they are to the query. 

I ask: "What does an embedding let a search system compare, and what must be true of the two things being compared?" What I am looking for is that the query and the passages are both converted by a compatible model and compared under a chosen measure of similarity. If you say it finds the right answer, I ask: "Who decides whether the top result is the right passage, the system or the lawyer?"

To make this visible, the next slide places our matter on an invented map.
02.11:
This slide has three clicks, and the map is invented for teaching. No embedding model produced these positions.

On the first click the query appears: restructuring consent. On the second the nearby candidates appear. The group exception candidate sits close, and on this slide it stands for the Key Terms change to Section 12.6, which requires consent to a change of control and excuses it for a reorganization within a wholly owned group. The support access clause sits somewhat near. On the third click the distant ones appear: the invoice payment term and photograph consent. The photograph item shares the word consent yet sits far away.

I ask: "Does this drawing prove how a real model would place these passages?" I am listening for no. We would need actual embeddings and a documented way of flattening them. If the answer is yes, I ask what we would have to run to find out.

The picture is flat, and the next slide explains what flattening costs.
02.12:
The three boxes explain why a flat picture needs care.

A real embedding has many numerical dimensions, often hundreds or more. We cannot draw that. So a drawing squeezes it into two dimensions. Think of a globe and a flat map of the world. The map is useful, and it still distorts distances, such as the size of far northern countries. A two-dimensional projection loses information in the same way. And the third box says the similarity score depends on the representation and on the method used to compare.

I ask: "Could we read one dimension of an embedding as a named legal concept, like liability?" A good answer says usually no, because learned dimensions have no simple label. If you say yes, I ask how we would check that claim, and what result would show it was wrong.

Now we look at a different limit. The same word can carry different representations in different sentences, and the next slide shows an example.
02.13:
Read the two sentences on the slide. "The bank registered a charge over the property" and "The prosecutor amended the charge." The word is the same. In the first it is security over land. In the second it is an accusation in court.

Older methods gave each word in the vocabulary a single fixed list of numbers. Modern language models build the representation from the surrounding tokens, so the representation of charge differs in the two sentences. The slide's last line says contextual representations depend on surrounding language.

I ask: "What in each sentence tells you which meaning of charge applies?" What I want to hear is the neighbouring words, bank, registered and property on one side and prosecutor and amended on the other, plus the task we are doing. If you point only to the word itself, I ask: "If I show you only the word charge and nothing else, what can you tell me?"

Context helps, yet closeness still does not settle legal meaning, and the next slide shows why.
02.14:
This slide is a caution about trusting closeness. I read the three boxes.

Related terms can have different legal effects. Approve and reject can appear in very similar contexts, so a system may rank them close together even though they mean opposite things. Take our own agreement. The Key Terms say neither party may assign without the other's prior written consent. A sentence saying a party may assign on notice, which is what the unmodified Standard Terms version of Section 12.6 allowed, looks very similar in vocabulary and has the opposite effect. 

I ask: "Give me a pair of clauses from a contract where one small change in wording reverses the result." Any real pair is fine. Consent and no consent is a good one. If you struggle, I offer the assignment example above and ask which of the two the Customer would prefer.

I am listening for the idea that similarity proposes candidates and the lawyer decides. 

The next slide steps back to show how a language model is built from start to use.
02.15:
This slide has four clicks, one for each stage. The first three sit under the heading that training can change parameters. The last sits under use.

The first click shows pretraining, where the model learns from broad data, mostly by predicting tokens. The second shows instruction tuning, where it is trained further to follow requested behaviour. The third shows preference learning, where feedback signals about better and worse answers shape it. The fourth shows inference, which means running the finished model on today's input. Inference does not itself run a training update.

I ask: "A colleague uploads Equator's agreement to a chat tool and gets an answer. Did that upload train the model?" A good answer says it supplied today's evidence for inference and changed no parameters. If you say yes, I ask: "If it had, what would the vendor have to do, and would we expect to be told?" Terms of any specific product are a separate contract question, and I do not state them here.

Next we move to the in-class exercises, where we test these ideas on our matter.
02.16:
This is our practice slide. It has four parts, and I run them in order. The guide gives about 15 minutes for the first demonstration and 25 for the guided work, with a break between.

First, I show six short document descriptions: a signed service agreement, employee terms, a credit note, a sales invoice, a privacy notice and a board approval. You sort them by type, and we then discuss how labels would be assigned for training. Second, we follow one numerical representation through the labelled network. Third, we place the query "consent for an internal restructuring of the provider" beside three candidates: the Key Terms change to Section 12.6, an invoice payment term, and the word consent in a photograph permission. Fourth, we test the idea that uploading an agreement equals training.

If a connected tool is unavailable, I use the labelled example, mark that step unexecuted and save the time for explanation. I rehearse any live step in the real account first.

You direct. Then we gather what we found on the next slide.
02.17:
Before I summarise, I ask you to give the conclusion in your own words. Then I compare it with the slide.

The first box says training adjusts parameters and inference uses them, tokens are input units, embeddings are numerical representations, and similarity proposes candidates without deciding legal equivalence. The second box says the coordinates and neural values we drew are illustrations and not measurements from a deployed model.

I ask: "Which part of today's picture would you not repeat to a client as a fact?" I am listening for the invented map and the schematic numbers. If you name nothing, I ask which figure on the similarity map we actually measured. The answer is none of them.

I write down any question still open, so we can return to it.

Now we turn the lesson into a decision for the firm, on the next slide.
02.18:
This is a class decision record. It does not authorise anything for the firm.

The proposed decision on the slide is to require vendors to explain training, source access and evaluation as separate matters. Training is what was done to the model before we got it. Source access is what documents the tool can read when we use it. Evaluation is how the vendor tested it. A vendor answer that blends the three tells us little.

I ask you to name one owner for this and one condition before it applies. For example, the owner could be the partner who signs off tools, and the condition could be that we receive the vendor's test method in writing.

I ask: "What evidence would change this proposed decision?" A good answer says we revisit it if the evidence, the quality or the permitted scope changes. If you have nothing, I ask what a vendor could show us that would make us ask fewer questions.

Then you test yourself on the next slide.
02.19:
I ask these three questions one at a time before I open the answer key, and I let you answer in full.

The first: "Does a token ID near another token ID establish similar meaning?" The answer I want is no. An ID names a piece of text, and nearby numbers need not mean nearby ideas. If you are unsure, I change arbitrary IDs on slide 22, such as swapping 285 and 914, and the words stay the same.

The second: "Why can charge mean security in one sentence and accusation in another?" I want context, the surrounding words, changing the representation.

The third: "What changes during training rather than ordinary inference?" I want parameters in training, and none in ordinary inference.

If an answer is partial, I return to the matching slide and ask the question again with a changed fact.

That ends the core of Session 2. Session 3 covers how language models generate answers and fail. If time is agreed, optional slides 20 to 25 follow.
02.20:
This optional slide shows what training data looks like. Each row has an input document and a target label: service terms and signature as a service agreement, employment terms as an employment agreement, invoice number and amount as an invoice. The footer says these three rows do not train or validate a classifier. A real one needs many more examples, and we keep later documents aside for the test.

I ask: "If someone mislabels an employment agreement as an invoice, what does the model learn from that row?" A good answer says it receives the wrong signal, and later predictions may be damaged. If you think one row is too small to matter, I ask how many mislabelled rows it would take, and who would notice.

Next, the optional slide on the neural network gives a plain definition of the term.
02.21:
This optional slide defines a neural network: a model made of connected computational units that transform inputs using parameters, usually with nonlinear functions. In plain words, each layer combines numbers and passes the result on. The nonlinear step lets later layers capture relationships that one straight-line rule cannot. It is computation. It is not a brain.

The box gives our case. An agreement classifier turns document features into scores for agreement and invoice, and the higher score wins.

I ask: "Must a partner understand matrix algebra to ask a vendor useful questions about a network like this?" A good answer says no. The partner needs to know the inputs, the learning signal, how it was evaluated and its limits. If you say yes, I ask which of those four questions need any algebra at all.

The next optional slide shows how words become the numbers that go into such a network.
02.22:
This optional table shows the path from words to model inputs. The sentence fragment is The provider remains responsible. Each schematic token gets an illustrative ID: 103, 285, 914 and 602. Each ID selects a learned list of numbers, the vector in the third column. The footer says the boundaries and IDs are invented, and that ID proximity does not measure meaning.

The ID works like a locker number. Locker 285 and locker 286 are neighbours in the corridor, and what is inside can be quite different.

I ask: "Are token IDs themselves a measure of meaning?" A good answer says no. An ID selects a representation, and the vector carries the learned information. If you hesitate, I ask whether renumbering the vocabulary would change what the words mean.

The sentence is a useful one to remember for Session 3, since the Key Terms exception to Section 12.6 says consent is not required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group if Provider remains responsible.

Next, the optional slide on foundation models.
02.23:
This optional slide defines a foundation model: a model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many later tasks, through prompting or further training. Prompting means giving it written instructions and material at the time of use. The box on the slide has one model summarising the client instruction and also drafting a proposed amendment.

Broad training is a strength for range. It tells us nothing yet about our own work. A model trained on broad text has not been shown to be reliable on current Ugandan tax law, and the slide's guide answer says domain relevance, current sources and testing on the task remain necessary.

I ask: "Does broad training establish expertise in current Ugandan tax law?" A good answer says no, and names current sources and a task test. If you say it has read everything, I ask when it was last updated and how we would find out.

The next optional slide lists the model families we may hear about.
02.24:
This optional slide is an overview of three architecture families, and I keep it short. An architecture is the way a model's parts are connected.

Transformers are central to current language systems. Convolutional networks often process spatial patterns, such as images, which is relevant to scanned pages. Recurrent architectures process a sequence step by step through a recurrent state. A product can combine several of these, so a scanned contract tool might use one family to read the page image and another to handle the text.

I do not go into how any of them work, since we are not building models.

I ask: "Which of these three matters most for our explanation of language models, and why might the product still use others?" A good answer picks transformers and notes that the wider system can include other models. If you pick all three equally, I ask which one reads text and which one reads the scanned page.

The last optional slide returns to something practical, which is what happens when the model changes.
02.25:
This optional closing slide connects the technical material to control. A new model can change extraction, wording and which tools it chooses. So after a material change, the firm repeats relevant tests. A good result under one model tells us nothing about the next version.

I ask: "If the provider updates the model next month, which tests from today would you keep and run again?" I am listening for representative agreements, questions where the source has no answer, the exception in the Key Terms version of Section 12.6, and the access rule the Key Terms add to Section 1.5 (each support person named in a written request and approved in writing first). If you name only one test, I ask what the other kinds of failure would look like.

This slide is the end of the optional material, so I finish by reminding you that Session 3 looks at how language models generate answers and how they fail.

03.1: Welcome to Session 3. Last session we looked at how a model learns. Today we look at what it does when it answers a question, and why a fluent answer can differ from one run to the next, leave out evidence or state a fact that no document supports. We finish with a reliability comparison on our own matter and a routine for checking answers.
03.2:
I open with the recall question before I show anything. I ask: "We upload a new clause today, for example the Section 12.6 change in the Key Terms. Which learned parameters must change?" A parameter is one of the numbers a model adjusted during training. I wait and let you reason it through.

A satisfactory answer says none need change. Training is finished. The clause arrives as input at the time of the request, which we call inference. If you say the model learns the clause, I ask: "When you close the chat and open a new one, what does the model still hold from this file?"

Then I put today's question on the screen: why can a fluent answer vary, omit evidence or invent a fact? The result we want is an observed comparison and a checking routine. Next I show how a prompt becomes a response.
03.3:
Here is the path from your question to the answer, in three steps. First, the application assembles what the model will see: instructions, your question and any documents it was given. Second, the model, which is the trained program, calculates a score for every possible next token. A token is a small piece of text, often a word or part of a word. Third, a decoding method picks one token, adds it to the text and the process repeats.

I ask: "Is the model normally choosing one finished answer from a shelf of prewritten answers?" A satisfactory answer says no. It produces the text piece by piece.

If you say it looks up an answer, I ask: "If it looked answers up, why would the same question come back worded differently?" Some products add search or tools before this step. The picture on the slide is the core mechanism. Now I show what those scores look like.
03.4:
Three clicks build this slide. The first shows the prefix: "The provider remains". The second shows the three candidate continuations, "responsible", "liable" and "available". The third shows the percentages, 70, 20 and 10. I say clearly that these numbers are invented for teaching. They are not from a real model.

The point is that the percentages describe how likely each word is as the next word. A sentence that reads well can still leave out a legal condition, such as the one about the group exception in Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms.

I ask: "Does 70% on this picture mean there is a 70% chance the legal advice is correct?" A satisfactory answer says no. The number belongs to the next word and says nothing about whether a legal claim is true.

If you agree with the 70%, I ask: "What source would tell you whether the sentence is true?" Next, we see how this repeats.
03.5:
Four clicks here. The first shows the current prefix, "The provider remains". The second shows the next-token scores and the choice of "responsible". The third shows the new prefix, "The provider remains responsible". The fourth shows the arrow that sends the updated prefix back for the next token.

The step to watch is that the answer so far becomes part of the input for the next word. If an early word leaves out a qualification, later words build on that. The model reads the signed contract only if the system has supplied it.

I ask: "Our question is whether Victoria's consent is needed. What would this prefix need in front of it before we trusted the next words?" A satisfactory answer names the current clause, meaning Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms, and the transaction facts.

If the answer is vague, I ask: "Which document would you hand it first?" Next, why one prompt can give different answers.
03.6:
Decoding is the rule for picking a token from the candidate scores. Because there is more than one possible pick, more than one response is possible. Temperature is a setting that can flatten or sharpen the scores. Many chat products do not show it, so I do not promise that your tool has the setting. Low randomness often favours the strongest candidates. It gives no proof of truth and no guarantee that two runs match.

I ask: "If three answers to the same question agree, have we verified the clause?" A satisfactory answer says no. Agreement between answers is a different thing from comparison with the agreement text itself.

If you say yes, I ask: "If all three read the wrong document, what would they agree on?" Today's run may show three matching answers, and that is a valid result. Next, how much the model can see at once.
03.7:
Three clicks. The first shows the box labelled active context, which holds what the model can use for this request. The second fills it with instructions, evidence and conversation. The third adds the output, because the answer being written also takes space. This is the context window: the amount of text the model can work with in one request. The proportions are conceptual. Each product sets its own rules for what goes in, what is summarised and what is dropped.

The note at the bottom matters. A file sitting in the application is not always in the window.

I ask: "A file is uploaded to the chat. Can it be available in the application and still absent from what the model used to write this answer?" A satisfactory answer says yes. Available, retrieved and in the window are three different states.

If you say no, I ask: "How would you find out which pages the answer used?" Next, what happens when the evidence does fit.
03.8:
This slide separates two problems. One is capacity, a hard limit on how much fits. The other is use, how well the model works with what does fit. A passage can sit inside the window and still be left out or misread.

Our agreement has a cross-reference. The Key Terms replace the Standard Terms' Section 12.6, and the Key Terms control. In class we compare answers from the whole agreement, from the Standard Terms only and from the focused excerpt. I do not promise a failure on any of them. A correct answer is a valid result.

I ask: "If the window is large enough to hold the whole agreement, do we still need to check the exception against the text?" A satisfactory answer says yes, because evidence that is present can still be misread or omitted.

If you say no, I ask: "What check would you do on the answer?" Next, how the model relates words to one another.
03.9:
Three clicks. The first shows the sentence "The provider remains responsible for its obligations." The second draws a link from "its" to "provider". The third adds a link to "responsible" and shows other words as other context. Attention is the step where the model weighs the other words in the text when it builds the meaning of each word. The weights come from the input, so the same word gets a different representation in a different sentence.

The links on the slide are invented for teaching. Attention depends on the input, the layer and the head, and it is not a record of the model's legal reasoning.

I ask: "In this sentence, what does 'its' point to, and how would you know?" A satisfactory answer says the provider, from the surrounding words.

If you say it shows how the model reasoned, I ask: "Who verified that these arcs match a real decision?" Next, what goes wrong.
03.10:
Hallucination is the word for generated content that is false, unsupported or inconsistent with the evidence. The model is trained to produce likely text. That goal does not require it to check each statement against a source. Missing sources, vague instructions and reasoning slips can each contribute, so I avoid giving one cause.

Take our matter. The signed Fee Schedule was not supplied to us. If an answer gives Victoria an annual fee figure, nothing in the evidence supports it.

I ask: "The model states the annual fee as a number. Which source would establish the amount?" A satisfactory answer says the signed Fee Schedule, which the supplied documents do not include.

If you say the contract in general, I ask: "Where in the Order Form does the fee figure live, and is that document in front of us?" Next, what can improve the answer.
03.11:
This table lists four things that can help and, in the last column, what is left to check. A reasoning-oriented mode spends more computation on a multi-step task, and the conclusion still needs checking against evidence. Search or retrieval brings in sources, and we check their authority, coverage and fidelity. A calculation tool executes the arithmetic, and we check which numbers went in and the formula. Human review adds professional judgment, and the reviewer needs competence and evidence.

An explanation in chat is a piece of generated text. It is not a transcript of the model's inner workings. I ask for a short justification, the source passage and a calculation I can repeat.

I ask: "Can a convincing explanation replace a missing source?" A satisfactory answer says no. We request the source or record the gap.

If you hesitate, I ask: "What would you write in the file note?" Next, different kinds of input.
03.12:
The three rows are three kinds of input. A text layer can be read and transformed, and the failure to inspect is a lost scope or exception. A scanned page is an image. The tool recognises the image or runs OCR, which means software that turns picture text into typed text, and the failure to inspect is a missing word or wrong reading order. A spreadsheet can be read as a table or calculated, and the risk is the wrong cells, units or formula.

An assistant that accepts images may use several components behind the screen. Session 5 tests extraction in detail. I only mention that OCR output on a poor scan broke the key consent sentence in the saved test output.

I ask: "The assistant has seen the page. Does that mean it extracted every clause accurately?" A satisfactory answer says no. We compare its output with the source.

If you say yes, I ask: "How would you spot one missing word?" Next, our three experiments.
03.13:
Now the demonstration. Before class I open Generation Experiments.txt and rehearse in the real account. I run the first task and keep the actual output. You then predict the others.

Experiment one asks: "Does Victoria's consent apply to Equator's proposed internal reorganisation? Quote the provisions you rely on, state what is unknown and list what we must ask Equator." I run it three times in new chats with the same evidence. Experiment two gives the whole agreement, then only the Standard Terms, which still contain the unmodified Section 12.6 and not the Key Terms, then only a short extract that contains the Key Terms change KT-1. The Standard-Terms-only run is expected to give a different answer because it cannot see the Key Terms, and that is a result about missing evidence. Experiment three asks for the annual Fees under the Order Form.

I ask: "What would be a successful answer to the missing-fee question?" A satisfactory answer says the amount is not established and asks for the signed Fee Schedule. If the tool is unavailable, I use the saved runs, say they are from one Claude model on one day (26 October 2026) with one run per condition except the three repeats, and mark the live step unexecuted. Next, cost.
03.14:
Four things drive what a workflow costs. Inputs and outputs are measured in tokens, and I use actual usage where the product reports it. Tools and repeated runs add calls, retries and set-up. Human checking is the minutes spent per acceptable result. Maintenance covers refreshing sources, testing and support.

I use Cost and Effort Example.csv. Its rates are invented for the exercise and are not any provider's prices. For example, the file assumes 40 tasks a month, 30 manual minutes and 20 assisted minutes, with a stress case of 33. I remind you that checking time belongs in the sum.

I ask: "A cheaper model needs two retries and a long correction on each matter. Could it cost more per reviewed matter than a dearer one?" A satisfactory answer says yes, because the cost that counts is per acceptable result.

If you pick the lowest token rate, I ask: "Where did the reviewer's minutes go in your total?" Next, our guided work.
03.15:
This is the in-class work, about 25 minutes. I show the first example and keep its actual output. You then predict which parts of the answer might vary and run the same fictional-source task in three new chats. Next you compare the whole agreement with the focused excerpt, and then asks for the annual fee. We score source fidelity and completeness apart from writing quality, and we retain the prompts and outputs in Generation Run Record.csv.

Before we start I ask: "Which parts of the answer do you expect to differ between the three runs, and which parts should stay the same?" A satisfactory answer expects wording and order to differ, and expects the quoted clauses and the list of unknown facts to stay.

If the account is unavailable, I use the saved runs, which are from one Claude model on one day (26 October 2026) with one run per condition except the three repeats, label the step unexecuted and keep time for the explanation. A correct or identical result is still a valid result. Next, what we can conclude.
03.16:
First I ask you to say the conclusion in your own words, before I read it. Then I compare it with the slide. Generation selects tokens conditioned on context. Responses can vary. Matching answers still need evidence checks. A larger context or a reasoning mode does not remove that need.

The second point is that the probabilities in our diagram were invented, and real behaviour and interface controls differ by product.

I ask: "Which part of today's result is still unverified?" A satisfactory answer names what we saw only once, such as three runs of one model, and the controls of your own tool. One run shows what happened once and gives no failure rate.

If you claim a general rate, I ask: "How many runs would you need before saying that?" I keep a list of open questions on the page. Next, the decision for the firm.
03.17:
This is a class decision record. It does not authorise anything for the firm. The proposed decision is to require source checking and measured review effort before the firm relies on a workflow. I write down a proposed owner and one condition for going ahead.

I ask: "What evidence would change this decision, for example in either direction?" A satisfactory answer names something observable, such as review minutes per matter from the cost file, errors found against the agreement text, or a change in the permitted scope of use. The decision is revisited if the evidence, the quality or the scope changes.

If you offer a feeling, I ask: "What would we measure to settle it?" We record the decision and the evidence still needed. Next, three questions to check what we covered.
03.18:
I ask the three questions before showing any answer, and you answer each in turn.

First: "The document never supplies a renewal fee. What should the answer say?" It should state that the fee is missing and request the source, here the signed Fee Schedule.

Second: "A longer context window includes the clause. Is the conclusion guaranteed?" No. Capacity is different from faithful use, so the answer is still compared with the text.

Third: "Three identical responses appear. What is the remaining verification?" You compare the proposition with the authoritative text and the facts.

If an answer is partial, I ask for the source that would support it. Next session, Session 4, covers AI tools, effective instructions and safe use.

04.1: Welcome. Today's question is on the slide: how do we select a tool, brief it clearly and verify a useful result? We work on the Kampala Legal and Tax matter for Victoria Services Ltd, and by the end we will have a reusable review brief and a recorded decision about a tool and its data. I start with a recall question before showing anything, so the next slide comes straight after this one.
04.2:
Before I explain anything, I ask the recall question from Session 3: three assistants repeat the same unsupported fee. What has been established? I wait for the full answer and ask for the reason.

I am listening for this. Three matching answers show that the agreement exists and that the assistants agree with each other. They do not show the fee, because the signed Fee Schedule was never supplied, so no source supports the number. Agreement between tools is a weak test.

If you say the fee is probably right, I ask: "Which document would you open to check it, and do we have it?"

Then I read today's question at the right of the slide and the result we are building, a reusable review brief and a documented tool and data decision. The next slide puts one question to several products, to see what a fair comparison needs.
04.3:
Here is the setup for comparing products. The question is the one on the slide: What does the agreement require for an internal reorganisation? In our agreement this is Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms. We give every product the same two sources, the executed agreement and the client instruction.

Products differ in many ways. One may read an uploaded file, one may search, they use different models and settings. If I change the question or the files between runs, I cannot tell what caused a difference. So I keep the inputs fixed and write down what each product actually did.

I ask: "If I gave one product the agreement and another only a summary of it, what could we conclude from the two answers?"

A good answer says nothing reliable, because the evidence differed. You may say the better product will cope anyway. I follow up: "How would we know it coped, if we never compared like with like?"

Next, the tool landscape shows the kinds of product we might compare.
04.4:
This slide is a short tour of categories, and the names are examples. They are not endorsements, and I do not claim any feature beyond what the table says. General assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are listed for drafting and work on files we supply. Legal platforms such as Harvey and NetDocuments are listed for precedents and document review. AlphaSense is listed for investment and industry research. Copilot Studio and Zapier are workflow builders, where the work is connections and review steps. An assistant is a program that answers instructions in ordinary language. Products and plans change, so I tell you I would check the vendor's current material before relying on any of it.

I ask: "A product calls itself a legal platform. What would you need to see before you believe it covers Ugandan law?"

I am listening for jurisdiction, which sources it holds, how they are updated, and testing on our own cases. A label proves none of these. If you accept the label, I ask which sources the product searches.

Now we turn to what must be settled before any real matter goes into a product.
04.5:
This table is a checklist I would run before any real matter goes into a product. I work down it with you. First, which product and which account, since consumer, business and API terms are different documents. Second, how the content is used, including any training choice and feedback. Third, where it is kept: chats, files, logs, backups and deletion. Fourth, who can see it, through workspace roles, connectors and subprocessors. The last row asks whether this matter may go in at all, and that is a firm decision under professional duties.

In class we use fictional records only. I open the official terms of the account we actually have, and I note anything the terms leave unanswered.

I ask: "A product says it does not train on your content. Does that tell you nobody keeps a copy or can open it?"

A good answer says no. Training, retention and access are separate questions with separate evidence. If you treat them as one, I ask: "Which row of the table would that setting answer?"

Next, a vague request next to a clear brief.
04.6:
Two requests on one slide. The vague one reads: "Review this contract and tell me if it is okay." I ask you what "okay" means here. Okay for whom, against what standard, and shown how? The tool has to guess, and so does the reader of its answer.

The clear request names the comparison, asks for the relevant passage in quotation, asks to preserve exceptions, and asks the tool to flag missing transaction facts. In our matter the passage is Section 12.6 as changed by the Key Terms, and the missing facts are the ownership chart and confirmation that Equator remains responsible.

I ask: "Which words in the clear request tell us how to judge the answer?"

I want to hear the quoted passage, the preserved exceptions and the flagged gaps, because a reviewer can check each of them. If you say the clear one is just longer, I ask: "Which sentence could you mark as met or missed?"

The next slide breaks a good brief into four parts.
04.7:
A brief has four parts, shown on the slide. Purpose and audience: what decision the work supports and who will read it. Evidence and boundaries: which sources apply and which do not. Output and acceptance criteria: what the answer looks like and how we will judge it. Questions, uncertainties and a review point: where the tool should stop and ask, and who looks next.

I use the picture of briefing a junior colleague, with one limit. A junior understands the client and answers for the work. A model has neither, so the brief mainly serves our checking and does not move accountability to the tool.

I ask: "Before a junior starts on the Equator question, what would you tell them?"

I am listening for the decision at stake, the agreement and instruction as the sources, the form of the answer, and when to come back with a question. If you give only the task, I ask: "How would the junior know what to do when a fact is missing?"

Next is a written instruction we can reuse.
04.8:
This is the working instruction, and I read all four lines aloud once. Use the supplied agreement and playbook only. Return the clause, the exact passage, the departure and a proposed amendment. Keep qualifications and ask about missing facts. Prepare a draft for partner review. I have it open as Review Instruction.txt for the class, and I do not present it as a prompt that works everywhere.

I ask you to improve one acceptance criterion, for example by saying that the quoted passage must come from Section 12.6 as replaced in the Key Terms and not from the unmodified Standard Terms.

Then I ask: "What should the tool do if the sources are silent on a point, such as the annual fee?"

A good answer says the sources do not establish it, and the tool asks for the signed Fee Schedule. You may suggest a better prompt will find the number. I ask: "Which signed document would the number come from?"

Next, how a finding links back to its evidence.
04.9:
Each row on this slide ties a finding to evidence and to a place. The first finding says the consent exception may apply, resting on a wholly owned group and the provider remaining responsible. The agreement supplies that wording, and the location column points to it; read that reference as Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms change. The second finding says ownership is unconfirmed, because the client gave no ownership chart, and that comes from the Client Instruction.

Different claims need different kinds of source. A contract shows what the words say. It cannot show how Equator is owned today.

I ask: "Can the agreement tell us how Equator is actually owned?"

What I want to hear is no, and that we need transaction evidence such as an ownership chart from the client or Equator. If you say the agreement mentions groups, so it probably covers it, I ask: "Does a rule about groups say whether this group exists?"

Next, one finding set beside its supporting passage.
04.10:
Two clicks build this slide. The first brings in the finding: the group exception may apply, so confirm ownership and continued provider responsibility. The second brings in the passage beneath it with the closing line about transaction facts.

The slide quotes the two sentences of the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6 that deal with change of control. The replacement also begins with the general assignment sentence. I read the full replacement from the agreement and check the slide against it.

I ask: "A tool gives a citation and a link. What do you check beyond whether the link opens?"

A good answer says to read the passage, confirm the version is the executed v2, and ask whether the passage supports the finding, including its exception. You may think a real-looking citation proves the point. I follow up: "Does the cited sentence say what the finding says it says?"

Next, the four stages we repeat on every task.
04.11:
Four clicks bring in the stages in order. Brief: task, sources and criteria. Produce: a draft linked to its sources. Check: the rule, the exception and the facts. Refine: correct the draft and test again. The Variant A line at the bottom is the changed fact we apply the cycle to.

Variant A is fictional. An unrelated buyer acquires control of Equator through a share sale. I stipulate a change of control outside any wholly owned group. Under Section 12.6 as replaced, Equator must obtain Victoria's prior written consent before the change takes effect, and the group exception does not apply. The unmodified Standard Terms would have let Equator assign on notice after a change of control, and the Key Terms change overrides that.

I run the brief and keep the output. If the tool is unavailable, I use the labelled example and mark this step unexecuted.

I ask: "On these facts, does the group exception apply?"

I want to hear no, and why. The next slide asks who decides after the draft exists.
04.12:
Three lines on this slide describe where human review begins. A named partner checks the source and the interpretation. The draft stays unapproved until that decision. External delivery needs the defined approval.

Be careful with the phrase human in the loop. It means a particular person looks at particular evidence and can reject the draft. A general instruction to be careful does nothing. In our matter the partner would open Section 12.6 as replaced, read the exception, and check whether the facts about Equator's ownership are in the file. We return to building this into a workflow in Session 9.

I ask: "What exactly is the partner deciding at that point?"

A good answer says whether the draft is supported by the sources and fit for its intended use. You may say the partner checks for mistakes. I follow up: "Which mistakes, against which document?"

Next, a check on tone, to catch fluent text that says nothing.
04.13:
Two drafts sit side by side. The weak one says the agreement "seamlessly safeguards stakeholders and unlocks compliance." It sounds confident and contains no source, no issue and no fact. The useful one names the group-reorganisation exception in Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms, and tells the reader to confirm ownership and continued provider responsibility before advising on consent.

I show how to repair the weak draft. Delete the praise, ask what the actual issue is, and ask which fact is missing. Smooth wording can hide a gap, since a model can write well with nothing behind it.

I ask: "Which of the two sentences could a client act on tomorrow, and why?"

I am listening for the second one, because it identifies the issue and the evidence still needed. If you prefer the first for its tone, I ask: "What would the client do after reading it?"

Next, a small scored check for the drafts we produce.
04.14:
Here is the checklist we use to judge a draft. Source accuracy: does the quote match the current clause? Completeness: does the answer keep the exception? Uncertainty: does it name the missing ownership facts? Usefulness: can the reviewer see the next action? I score each from 0 to 2 using Evaluation Rubric.txt. A critical error fails the draft whatever the total: a restricted disclosure, an invented material term or a lost operative exception.

This is guided application. You direct the changed example, and I score the saved output together with you. We keep the real responses, since one run shows what happened once and says nothing about how often.

I ask: "A draft scores 6 out of 8 but quotes the old unmodified Section 12.6. Do we accept it?"

No. A wrong source version is a critical error. If you accept it because of the score, I ask which row of the table that error falls under.

Next, questions to put to a vendor.
04.15:
This table is our list of questions for a vendor, one row per area. Legal coverage: jurisdictions, sources, updates and exclusions. Evaluation: representative cases, errors and review effort. Data: terms, access, retention, location and deletion. Operations: integrations, support, logs and exit. Commercial: total costs, limits and change terms. We ask for evidence in each row and do not accept a statement as an answer.

I treat a sales demonstration as a claim to test. A product can have a feature that this particular account has not switched on, so I ask which one we would receive.

I ask: "After a convincing sales demonstration, what would you request before buying?"

A good answer asks for a controlled trial on permitted, representative cases, with tests agreed in advance and a written review of the data terms. You may say the demonstration was enough because the output looked right. I follow up: "What would the vendor show us if the next case were harder?"

Now we do the in-class work.
04.16:
Now we work, and this block carries most of the session. I show the first example and keep its real output. There are four steps. First, inspect the account we actually have and record unanswered data-use questions, entering no client data. Second, run the vague request and then the professional brief on the same fictional text. Third, change to Variant A, the unrelated buyer acquiring control of Equator by share sale. Fourth, score the result and record a procurement question the demonstration cannot answer.

You predict the answer, choose the evidence, and check the changed example. I save each output or mark that step unexecuted.

Rehearse this in the real account before class. If the connected tool is unavailable, I use the labelled example, mark the step unexecuted and keep time for the explanation.

I ask: "Before we run it, what do you expect the tool to say for Variant A?"

Next, what we can conclude from this work.
04.17:
Let me ask you to state the conclusion first, then I compare it with the slide. For Variant A, the group exception does not apply and Section 12.6 as replaced requires Victoria's prior written consent. A useful brief names sources, task, output, gaps and review. Data terms need inspection of the actual account.

The second point limits it. A tiny class comparison does not rank providers and does not authorise use of a real client matter.

I ask: "Which part of today's result is still unverified?"

I want to hear that we have compared a few runs on fictional records, so we know nothing about reliability across many cases, and nothing yet about the firm's approval for real data. If you say the tool passed, I ask: "How many times did we run it?"

The next slide records the firm decision.
04.18:
This slide holds the decision we record. The proposal is to evaluate one available tool on a permitted task before selecting a subscription or integration, and to write down the evidence still needed. I name an owner and one condition before we proceed. This is a class record and does not authorise the firm to do anything.

I ask: "What evidence would change this proposed decision?"

A good answer names results that would move it: weak performance on permitted cases, data terms that fail the checklist, or a change in the permitted scope. The decision is then revisited. If you say we should buy the tool now, I ask what we learned that justifies a subscription.

Next, three questions that check what we have covered.
04.19:
Three questions, asked before I open the key. First: an unrelated buyer acquires control of Equator. Does the group exception in the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6 apply? Second: the account is paid. May the firm upload any matter? Third: a prompt asks for a citation. What makes it useful?

For the first, I am listening for no. The share sale is outside the group, so Equator needs Victoria's prior written consent before the change takes effect. For the second, price does not settle permission. The firm checks the account terms, how the data is processed and its own authority. For the third, a useful citation points to the exact passage, and we check authority, version and fit.

If an answer is partial, I ask: "Which document would settle that?"

The next session turns to preparing the firm's information, where the files and sources a tool reads get organised. Slides 20 to 24 are optional extras.
04.20:
This optional slide uses legal document review as a market example. It says Harvey combines document review, drafting and workflows, and NetDocuments offers source-linked comparison across document collections. I take these from the slide and do not add features. If I show vendor material, I say it is a vendor demonstration and not a live run of ours.

I ask: "Before a partner buys a product like this, what must be verified?"

I am listening for coverage, permissions, output quality, integration, support and total cost. If you are impressed by the demonstration, I ask which collection of documents the feature searches. Then we return to the closing check.
04.21:
This optional slide describes knowledge search in a firm: find a precedent the team may already hold, compare clauses across authorised agreements, and open the original passage before relying on the answer. NetDocuments is a market example. The firm does not need it for the lesson to apply. Sessions 5 and 6 explore how this works.

I ask: "When the tool summarises a precedent, what is the source of truth?"

A good answer says the authoritative document and the applicable facts. A generated summary is a pointer. If you trust the summary, I ask: "What would you open to confirm it?" Then we return to the closing check.
04.22:
This optional slide shows investment research as a transfer example. AlphaSense is described as offering multi-step research over its available content. A partner could investigate a sector or compare investment claims. What the report can establish depends on source access and relevance. It extends the evidence-checking method from our matter.

I ask: "A report arrives with one hundred citations. Does that prove its conclusion?"

I want to hear no. Check coverage, authority, and whether each passage supports its claim. If you say that many sources must be right, I ask how many of the hundred we have opened. Then we return to the closing check.
04.23:
This optional table lists adjacent uses. They are proposed designs for discussion. They do not claim that a deployed product does them. Fintech: a regulatory-change evidence brief, with the boundary at qualified interpretation and source dates. Telco: complaint themes and contract obligations, bounded by access and individual treatment. Investments: compare claims with source records, bounded by diligence and the investment decision.

I ask: "Which of these three share the same underlying steps?"

A good answer says each retrieves sources, extracts facts, classifies them, writes a draft and then needs review. If you treat the sectors as unrelated, I ask what the review step looks like in each. Then we return to the closing check.
04.24:
This optional slide is about examples and output structure. A completed example shows what we mean. A table makes omissions visible. A schema, which is a fixed layout of named fields, constrains structure while the facts still need checking. Session 5 introduces JSON as named fields and values, and Session 9 reuses that structure in a tool request.

I show one row: a source quote in one field and an unknown fact in another.

I ask: "A table is fully filled in. Does that mean the review is complete?"

A good answer says no, because the quote and the interpretation still need checking. If you rely on the tidy layout, I ask you to pick one cell and verify it against Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms.

05.1:
Welcome to Session 5. Today's question is what the firm holds, and what has to happen to it before an AI tool can use it reliably. By the end we will have a source inventory and one extraction that we have checked against the original page, with its provenance recorded.

I keep the opening short. The first ten minutes belong to the recall question on the next slide, and I ask it before I explain anything.
05.2:
Before I show any answer, I ask the question on the slide: "In Session 4 we wrote an instruction that asks for exact quotes. What happens if the scan that feeds that instruction has lost a word?" I wait and let you reason it through. This block takes about ten minutes with the title slide.

I am listening for the idea that a good instruction cannot recover a word that was never captured. Careful wording cannot fill a gap in the input, so the source has to be inspected. If the answer is only "the model would guess", I ask: "Would you be able to tell from the answer that it guessed?"

Then I read out today's question and the result we are building: an inventory and an inspected extraction with provenance.

The next slide starts with the firm's actual sources, so we can see where scans and files sit in the records room and the shared drive.
05.3:
This slide shows four kinds of source: paper files and scans, digital files such as agreements and email, and systems such as a document management system and accounting. They are categories to walk through and are not stages in a sequence. We list every source first and choose how to prepare it afterwards.

I do not assume which system the firm uses. I ask you to describe your own landscape in your words, and I write down the systems and the pain points as you name them, without client names.
