I ask: "Where does a piece of advice the firm has already given become hard to find today, and where does it sit when that happens?"

A good answer names a real place, such as a box of signed originals, a shared drive folder or an email thread, and says why it is hard to find. Your answer sets the inventory priority for the rest of the session.

The next slide gives us four ways to describe any one of these sources.
05.4:
A source has four separate properties. Location or system is where it lives, such as the records room, a drive or a database. Modality is what kind of content it is: text, a document image or audio. Structure is how it is organised: a table, semi-structured fields or narrative. Format is the file type, such as DOCX, PDF, CSV, JSON or XML.

I keep the four apart on purpose. A spreadsheet in the drive is one location, one format, and it can hold both a structured table and free notes.

I ask: "Is every PDF made of text that a computer can search?"

I am listening for no. A PDF can hold selectable text, a picture of a page, or both. If you say yes, I ask you to think of a scanned signed agreement saved as a PDF and say what the computer actually holds.

That scanned PDF is the next slide: a page image beside searchable text.
05.5:
The picture shows an authored page, a synthetic scan of it and the saved OCR output. OCR means optical character recognition: software that reads an image of text and returns characters. The slide says searchable text is useful only if the rule, negation, exception and condition survive.

I have the observed run open. It is Tesseract 4.1.1 on the page for CONTRACT-01 v2, Section 12.6 as the Key Terms replace it (KT-1). The clean image and the synthetic scan both read correctly. The moderate degraded scan gave "That consent not sequel fF 2 reorganization", so the condition was lost. That is one run on one page.

I ask: "If I search this text for the word consent and it finds a hit, what have I proved?"

A good answer says only that the word is present. It does not show that the sentence around it, with its exception, was captured correctly. I ask you to find the damaged words.

Next we ask what the firm should record about every source.
05.6:
Each source needs four facts recorded. Who is the matter and information owner. Which version is authoritative, and from what effective date. Who may read it, and for what use. And who is responsible for updating, retaining and disposing of it.

Access belongs in the design from the start. If we add it at the end, copied content may already be in the wrong hands.

I ask: "In our matter, who should decide which agreement is the authoritative one for Victoria Services Ltd, and why that person?"

What I want to hear is the matter owner or a qualified person the owner designates. A tool and a filename do not settle authority. If you name the person who happens to hold the file, I ask: "Would that person know whether a later version was signed?"

The next slide fills these four facts in for four sources from our matter.
05.7:
The table has four rows. CONTRACT-01 v2 is the executed agreement, so we extract it and verify its clauses. Draft v1 is superseded context, so we label it and keep it out of default answers. The September ledger is financial evidence, so we check fields, period and units. A public judgment is a candidate legal authority, so we check court, date and treatment.

The role decides how a search tool should treat each source. The same filename can sit in two folders and hide two versions.

I ask: "Would you delete Draft v1 as soon as v2 was signed?"

A good answer follows the retention policy and keeps the draft's history while making sure it does not answer current questions. If you would delete it, I ask what you would show a colleague who asks how the Section 12.6 wording changed.

Next we follow a source through the steps that prepare it, one click at a time.
05.8:
This slide has four clicks. The first reveals Capture, where we scan or retrieve the source. The second reveals Extract, where we get text and layout. The third reveals Check, where we compare the original against the extract. The fourth reveals Represent, where we add structure and metadata.

This pipeline only prepares content. Searching it at question time is Session 6. At each click I ask what evidence should survive that step: the image, the text, the check result, the identifiers.

I ask: "Which of these four steps could change the legal meaning of a clause, and how?"

I am listening for any of the first three. A poor capture can drop a line, extraction can misread a word, and a missed check lets either through. Representation can also detach a quote from its source. If you pick one step only, I ask what happens when the earlier steps went wrong.

The next slide separates what the word OCR covers from the other parts of extraction.
05.9:
Three things sit in this slide. OCR converts images of text into machine-readable text. Layout analysis finds the parts of a document, such as headings, tables and paragraphs, and how they relate. Structured extraction takes chosen content and places it in defined fields, such as party name or date.

A document tool often combines all three, so a product's name for itself tells us little about what it covers.

I ask: "If a vendor says its product does OCR, does that tell you the clause numbers and table cells will come out in the right places?"

A good answer says no. OCR recognises characters, and layout and field extraction need their own checks. If you say yes, I show the three lines again and ask which one deals with a table cell and its column.

The next slide shows what layout analysis looks like in a vendor's documentation example.
05.10:
The picture is from Microsoft's Document Intelligence documentation. It is a reference screenshot of a product example and is not a run on our files. It shows text blocks, sections and a table picked out on a page.

The left caption says OCR recovers readable text: characters and words. The right says headings, tables and reading order keep context. Take a table of fees. A number such as 5,000,000 must stay tied to its row, its column, its unit and its period, or it means nothing.

I ask: "In a ledger table, why does reading the characters correctly still leave a number unusable?"

What I want to hear is that the number must stay with its row, column, currency and period. If you say the OCR was accurate, I ask what you would conclude if every figure moved up one row.

Now we return to our own agreement to see a damaged extract that changes a legal result.
05.11:
This slide puts two texts side by side. On the left is the authoritative wording, from the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6: "That consent is not required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group if Provider remains responsible for its obligations under this Agreement." On the right is a damaged extract: "That consent is required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group."

I say plainly that the damaged extract was prepared by hand as an exercise. It is a constructed example and has no connection to any OCR measurement.

I ask you to find both changes. The word "not" is gone, and the condition about the provider remaining responsible is gone. The meaning has reversed.

I then ask: "Could a better prompt bring back the missing words?"

A good answer is no. If the evidence is missing from the input, no instruction can reconstruct it reliably, and we must re-extract or go back to the original. If you hesitate, I ask how the model would know what the page said.

Next we put the original page on screen beside the extract.
05.12:
The picture is the rendered original page from our fictional agreement. Below it is the damaged extract again: "That consent is required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group." The slide asks which wording disappeared.

This is the worked demonstration, about twenty minutes across this slide and the next two. I put the page and the extract next to each other and run my finger along the heading, the Section 12.6 reference (the Key Terms replacement), the negation and the exception. I keep the page and section reference in the extracted record. If the image will not display, I use the labelled example from the guide and mark that step unexecuted.

I ask: "Before we put any of this text into a search tool, which checks must pass?"

A good answer includes that the text is complete, the reading order is right, the key wording is present, and the source location is recorded. If you list only spelling, I ask what a perfectly spelled wrong sentence would pass.

Next we record what we found in a document quality record.
05.13:
The record has four lines. Preserve the original. Record the defect and the corrected version. Keep the source location and the reviewer. Keep uncertain fields unresolved. I have the Document Quality Record file open and fill one row live for the damaged extract: the defect is the dropped "not" and condition, with the corrected text and the location, the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6.

A correction must never overwrite the only copy of the original. A confidence score from OCR cannot settle the legal effect either, because it measures reading and says nothing about what the clause means.

I ask: "An amount in the ledger scan is smudged and could be 1,800,000 or 7,800,000. What do we write in the record?"

What I want to hear is that the field is marked unknown until better evidence arrives, such as the original document. If you pick the likelier figure, I ask who would bear the cost of a wrong guess.

After the break we turn to the formats we store the corrected text in.
05.14:
This slide lists four representations and the job of each. Markdown keeps headings and document text readable. JSON holds named fields and structured outputs. Akoma Ntoso XML is a legal structure that carries identifiers and metadata. A CSV or database table suits repeated financial or matter records.

Converting a file to a new format does not make its content reliable. And no single format is required by every AI system. We pick the one that suits the use.

I ask: "Would you convert every private contract in the firm into Akoma Ntoso?"

A good answer is no. Choose a representation that fits the use and the system; for one agreement a simple record with exact text and source location may be enough. If you say yes, I ask what the firm would gain for a contract nobody will publish.

Next we take one clause and write it as a structured record.
05.15:
The left panel is the source and the right panel is a JSON record. JSON is a text format for named fields. Each key names a field and each value holds its content: document_id is the key and CONTRACT-01 is the value. The slide abbreviates the text. The slide labels the source Key Terms KT-1, which is the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6, and I say that aloud as I point at the record.

The record holds the document id, the version v2, the section, the exact passage and the source location. The passage has to be a verbatim copy. Each field is something a program can check.

I ask: "Which fields stop a quoted passage from losing its link to the agreement it came from?"

I am listening for the document id with the version and the source location. If you name only the text, I ask how a reader would find the page again in a year.

Now we ask who is allowed to see these records as they travel through the system.
05.16:
This slide has four clicks. The first reveals source access: matter permissions on the original. The second reveals copied content, which has to carry restriction metadata. The third reveals search results, filtered for the user asking. The fourth reveals the answer, built from allowed evidence only.

Search tools often work from a copy of the source. The copy can drift out of step with the permissions on the original. Our tests have to include a change of access, a deletion and a withdrawn document.

I ask: "A lawyer is taken off the Victoria Services matter after the files are indexed. What has to happen before the tool can answer their next question?"

A good answer says the access change must reach the copy and the search results, so no restricted passage comes back. If you say the original permission is enough, I ask where the copy lives and who updates it.

The next slide sets out the work we do together now.
05.17:
This is our in-class work, about thirty-five minutes of guided application after the break. I demonstrate the first example, and then you predict, pick the evidence and check the changed example. Four tasks: inventory systems, formats, owners and access; compare the original, the synthetic scan and the observed OCR; mark omissions against the authoritative page; and record corrections, provenance and update responsibilities.

I open the Information Inventory and add one row per system we actually discuss, with no client names. The observed OCR file is the one I use. If a live OCR or connected tool is unavailable, I use the labelled example, mark that step unexecuted and spend the time on explanation. A real run of any tool gets saved with its output.

I ask: "Which row of the inventory would you complete first, and what evidence would you need for it?"

I want a row tied to a real system and a named owner.

Then we write down what the work shows.
05.18:
I ask you to give the conclusion in your own words before I read the slide. Then we compare. The first point is that system, modality, structure and format describe four different properties, extraction must keep the negation, exception and condition, and originals and access details travel with every converted copy. The second is that a synthetic scan tests a method and says nothing about how well extraction would do on the firm's own archive.

I ask: "Which part of today's result is still unverified?"

What I want to hear is the archive. We tested one authored page, with one OCR run on it, and the firm's real documents would need their own sample. If you say everything is verified, I ask you how many real firm documents we tried.

I write down any open question. The next slide turns the result into a decision.
05.19:
The proposed decision reads: assign source owners and choose one collection for preparation before buying a search layer. I ask you to name a proposed owner and one condition, and I record both along with the evidence we still need. This is a class decision record and carries no firm authority.

I ask: "What evidence would make you change this decision?"

A good answer names something concrete, such as a sample of the chosen collection showing that most documents are scans too poor to read, a change in who may see the material, or a quality check that fails. The decision stands until the evidence, the quality or the permitted scope changes.

If you give a general answer, I ask you to name the first document you would test.

The next slide has three questions that check what we covered.
05.20:
I ask these three before I open the key. First: "The scan says shall not disclose, and the extraction says shall disclose. Which stage failed?" Second: "The text is accurate but the matter tag is wrong. What risk remains?" Third: "Which record keeps the correction history?"

For the first I want extraction, the stage that reversed the meaning. For the second I want a wrong tag to cause a passage to reach a user without access to that matter, or the wrong matter to be retrieved. For the third I want the source-linked document quality record, with the derived content tested again after each correction.

If you are unsure on the second, I ask which user would receive the passage.

That closes the session. In Session 6 we take prepared sources and see how a search tool finds the right passage in them.
05.21:
This optional slide is for a useful question or extra time. It shows a short XML fragment in the Akoma Ntoso style: a section with an identifier, a heading "Change of control" and the clause text. It is an illustrative fragment and is not a complete document that has been checked against the schema.

Legal publishers may supply structured originals like this, with sections, identifiers and versions that systems can follow.

I ask: "When would structured legal XML help a firm?"

A good answer is when sections, identifiers and versions of legislation have to be kept consistent across systems. For a single private agreement a plain record is often enough. If we are short on time, I go back to the closing check.
05.22:
This optional slide covers a ledger. Four questions apply to any financial field. Amount and currency: is it UGX, another currency or mixed? Period: is the date the invoice date, the service period or the receipt date? Missing value: is it unknown, not applicable or zero? Record identity: is a repeat a genuine repeat or a duplicate import?

If time allows I open Invoice Import.csv and find the repeated invoice. We do not clean any record before we know what it means.

I ask: "If a fiscal document number is missing from a row, does that mean no sale took place?"

A good answer is no. It raises a question about the evidence, and the transaction stays in the data until we answer it. If you say delete it, I ask what the tax return would then omit.
05.23:
This optional slide separates three jobs. Extracting party names and dates finds spans of text. Keeping document identity and version as metadata ties each passage to its source. Resolving which legal entity a name denotes links different mentions to one real company.

In our matter the two parties are Victoria Services Ltd and Equator Systems Ltd. A tool that finds both names has not yet established which registered company each one is.

I ask: "If two companies have similar names, does that show they are the same legal entity?"

A good answer is no. We check identifiers and authoritative records. If you are unsure, I ask what in the company register would settle it. If time is short, we return to the closing check.
05.24:
This optional slide turns the inventory into a question for an executive. Which collection offers the greatest useful opportunity? Who can establish its authority and quality? What preparation and permission work is needed first?

I ask: "If most of the firm's precedents are scans, what would you fund first?"

A good answer is the inventory, the choice of sources and reliable capture, ahead of a broad knowledge assistant. I record a realistic owner and a scope. If you want to start with the tool, I ask what it would read.

This closes the optional material. Session 6 begins with the search layer.

06.1: Welcome back. Last session we prepared the firm's documents. Today we look at what happens when someone asks a question of that prepared collection, and how the assistant finds the right passage and then writes an answer from it. The question on the screen is the one we work to: how does the assistant find current permitted evidence and use it faithfully? By the end we will have scored a retrieval test and read one source-linked answer.
06.2:
I ask the recall question before I say anything about the answer. I ask: "Last session we had two readable versions of the Equator agreement, the executed v2 and the earlier draft v1. Beyond the text itself, what must a retrieval system know about each one?"

I am listening for four things: which version is authoritative, which matter it belongs to, who is permitted to see it, and whether it has been updated or withdrawn. If you say only "which is newer", I ask: "Newer by date, or the one that was signed?" That brings out the status field.

Then I read out today's question and the result we are working toward: a scored retrieval test and a source-linked answer.

The question we asked last time comes back on the next slide, now put to an assistant that has to find its own evidence.
06.3:
This is the question from our matter, with a small correction to the wording on the slide. The operative text is the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6 (the course calls it KT-1), which overrides the unmodified Section 12.6 in the Standard Terms. The question is whether Victoria must consent when Equator reorganises. The collection holds the executed agreement and an older draft, so the assistant has two candidates that both look like "the agreement".

I ask: "If you were the assistant, and both documents mention reorganisation, what makes one passage the right passage?"

What I want to hear is relevance to the question, authority (the signed version), the current version, and permission for this user to see it. A good answer names more than relevance alone. If you say "the one that matches the words best", I ask: "The draft matches the words well. Why is it still the wrong source?"

Now we separate two things that a chat window blurs together: finding documents, and writing an answer.
06.4:
A search tool and an assistant that writes answers look alike in a chat window, so I separate them. Search returns documents or passages, and the person reads them. A generated answer is new text written by a language model (a model is a program that has learned patterns from large amounts of text and writes the next words) using whatever information was selected for it. That text needs checking.

I ask: "Suppose the search returns the correct Section 12.6 text (the Key Terms replacement), and the answer still comes out wrong. How could that happen?"

A good answer says the model can leave out a qualification from correct evidence, for example the group exception, or add a fact that no source gives. Some learners think correct search results guarantee a correct answer. If so, I ask: "Who reads the evidence before you rely on the sentence?"

That gap between finding and writing is exactly what the next slide names as a method.
06.5:
RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation. In plain words, the system first looks up relevant source material, then hands that material to the language model together with the question, and the model writes the answer from it. In our matter, it retrieves the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6 (KT-1) and, when we want the history, the unmodified Section 12.6 it replaced, supplies them with the question, and the model drafts a consent analysis.

I ask: "When the system supplies the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6 to the model, has the model learned the firm's files?"

A good answer is no. The model's parameters, the numbers it set during training, do not change. The evidence is placed in front of it for this one question and is gone afterwards. Many people assume RAG means the model was trained on firm files. If I hear that, I ask: "If we deleted the agreement from the library tomorrow, would the model still know it?"

The next slide shows the two separate paths that make this work.
06.6:
This slide has eight clicks, and it shows two paths that run at different times. The first four clicks cover preparing the collection. Click one shows documents, only current and permitted ones. Click two splits them into chunks, pieces of text with their source details. Click three shows an embedding model turning each chunk into a list of numbers, called a vector, so that similar meanings can be compared. Click four shows the index, storing vectors with metadata.

The last four clicks cover answering a question. Click five turns the question into a vector. Click six retrieves and filters the passages the user may see. Click seven passes the question and evidence to the language model. Click eight shows the answer with sources for review against the original.

I ask: "If the index returns draft v1, will a stronger answer-writing model repair that?"

A good answer is no. Choosing the right source is a separate job from writing. If you expect a smarter model to fix it, I ask: "If it only sees v1, where could it learn the group exception?"

Next, we look at how chunking can split a rule from its exception.
06.7:
This slide has two clicks. The first click shows a bad split: Chunk A holds "Provider must obtain Customer's prior written consent before a change of control takes effect." and Chunk B holds "That consent is not required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group ..." on its own. The second click shows the preserved version, where the rule, the exception and the responsibility condition sit together with the source name and location.

I ask: "Which question from a client would expose the bad split?"

What I want to hear is something like "Does an internal group reorganisation need Victoria's consent?" The words "That consent" point back to the sentence in Chunk A, so Chunk B has nothing to refer to once the two are apart, and that is why the split is harmful. If the search returns only Chunk A, the answer says consent is required, which leaves out the exception that the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6 (KT-1) contains. If it returns only Chunk B, the condition is lost. Chunk size is a design choice, and we test it against the questions the firm will ask.

If you think smaller chunks are always better, I ask: "What does a very small chunk lose from this clause?"

The next slide lists what every chunk should carry with it.
06.8:
A chunk is the unit that retrieval hands to the model. The slide lists four things it should keep. First, the relevant text and its relationships, so a rule travels with its exception. Second, the document identity and current version, so we know it is CONTRACT-01 v2. Third, the clause or page location, so a reader can find it again. Fourth, the matter permissions, so the system knows who may see it.

I ask: "Suppose a chunk says 'Consent is required unless the Provider's group exception applies,' and the term 'group' is defined three pages earlier. What do we do?"

A good answer is to retrieve or link the definition along with the chunk, because the clause cannot be read correctly without it. Some learners assume each chunk stands alone. I ask: "Would you advise a client from one sentence with its definition removed?"

Now we look at two ways of searching for these chunks.
06.9:
There are two basic ways to find a passage. Keyword search looks for exact words or identifiers, such as CONTRACT-01 or the phrase "change of control". Semantic search uses the vectors we met earlier to find text with a related meaning, so a question about a "group restructuring" can find a clause that says "reorganization".

I ask: "A partner types the exact record number RECORD-03 into the assistant. Which method helps most, and why?"

What I want to hear is keyword or identifier matching, because a number has no meaning to compare, only characters to match. Semantic search could return a nearby record that reads similarly. In the other direction, keyword search would miss "restructuring" if the clause only says "reorganization". You may say semantic search is simply the better method. I ask: "When would the exact words matter more than the meaning?"

In our scripts there is a check called negation_check.py. It asks for a statement and its opposite, for example "consent is required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group" and "consent is not required ...". With lexical word matching the two questions returned the same chunks in the same order in the saved run, whether the negation words were kept or dropped. This is one saved run on 40 documents. Ranking by similarity finds candidates. A person or the model has to read the passage to see which way it points.

The next slide combines the two methods into one pipeline.
06.10:
This slide has four clicks, and it builds a hybrid system. Click one shows the question, which has terms and a meaning. Click two shows the candidates, a pool of results from keyword search and from vector search together. Click three shows ranking, where the two lists are merged and reranked, meaning a second step puts the passages in a better order. Click four shows the evidence, the few passages that go to the model. I use only illustrative rankings and no invented scores.

I ask: "What happens if the right source never enters the candidate pool?"

A good answer says reranking only reorders what it receives, so it cannot bring back a missing document. The candidate stage has to supply it. If you think a good ranker rescues a poor search, I ask: "Where in the four steps would you check for the missing source first?"

Next is a prepared trace of this process for our matter, and I will say clearly what it is.
06.11:
This table comes from Retrieval Trace.txt, which is a prepared teaching trace. It is not a live search run, and the slide says so. I say that out loud before I read the rows. Draft v1 is superseded, so it gives historical context only. Executed v2 is current and permitted, so it supports the answer. OTHER-02 belongs to a restricted unrelated matter, so it is excluded before anything reaches the model.

I ask: "Which candidate supports the current answer, and which other piece of evidence do we need to add?"

I am listening for executed v2, with the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6 (KT-1) and the unmodified Section 12.6 it replaced, plus the Client Instruction for the ownership and responsibility facts that are missing. If you pick all three because they all mention change of control, I ask: "What does the status column tell you about each one?"

With the evidence chosen, the next slide shows the answer built from it.
06.12:
This slide has two clicks. The first click shows the finding: the group exception may apply, and we need to confirm ownership and continued provider responsibility. The second click shows the source text. The slide labels it "CONTRACT-01 v2, Key Terms KT-1", which is Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms. I read the quote exactly as printed.

I ask: "What does this clause not tell us, so we cannot yet say whether consent is needed?"

A good answer is that the clause gives the wording, and the transaction facts are separate. We do not have Equator's ownership chart, written confirmation that Equator remains responsible, or a statement on whether the agreement will move to another entity. Those are listed in the Client Instruction. You may think a quoted clause settles the client's case. I ask: "Which sentence of the answer is a quote, and which is the model's inference?"

Next we look at the two different ways this process can go wrong.
06.13:
There are two failures here and they need different fixes. In a retrieval failure, the system returns draft v1 as the governing agreement. The answer may read well and still rest on the wrong document. In a generation failure, the system finds v2 and then leaves the group exception out of its answer.

I ask: "A partner tells you the assistant gave a wrong answer on reorganisation consent. What do you look at first?"

What I want to hear is the retrieved evidence, meaning which documents and passages came back, before changing any instruction to the model. If v1 came back, a better prompt will not help. If v2 came back and the exception is missing, the fault is in the answer step. Some learners reach for a stronger model first. I ask: "How would you tell, in two minutes, which of the two failures you have?"

Having separated the failures, we now add a third control, which is who is allowed to see what.
06.14:
This slide has four clicks. Click one asks who is asking, which is identity. Click two applies a filter on the matters that person may see. Click three retrieves only permitted passages. Click four responds with a source-linked answer. The order matters: the filter works before retrieval, so restricted text never reaches the model.

I ask: "A senior partner who is not on the Victoria matter asks for the change-of-control clause in another client's agreement. Should the executive role get it automatically?"

A good answer is no. Access follows the actual authorised policy for that matter. Seniority does not override it. I also ask you to think about titles and metadata. Even a document title such as another client's name can reveal something confidential, so the test checks content and titles. If you assume rank opens every door, I ask: "Who decides who is on a matter, and where is that recorded?"

Next, we turn all of this into a short list of tests.
06.15:
This table is a set of tests for the firm assistant. Each row names a situation and the behaviour we expect. A current clause request returns v2 with the exception. A request for old wording labels the draft status. A missing transaction fact gets a question or an "unknown". A restricted matter withholds restricted evidence. A source update uses the amended evidence after a refresh.

I ask: "Suppose the assistant passes ninety-five percent of its tests. What could that high total be hiding?"

What I am listening for is a single serious failure, for example one access leak or one invented conclusion, which a total score smooths over. So we record the expected passages and score retrieval and answer fidelity separately, and we treat a critical failure as a failure however the total looks. The partner and a domain reviewer agree the acceptance rules. You may treat the average as the decision. I ask: "Which single failure would stop the pilot, whatever the score?"

Tests only help if the collection stays in good order, which is the next slide.
06.16:
A knowledge assistant is an information service that someone has to maintain. The slide lists four duties. An owner approves new and amended sources. Withdrawals and access changes reach the derived content, which means chunks and vectors made from a source change when the source changes. Tests run after material changes. Users can inspect sources and report mistakes.

I ask: "The assistant gives the wrong-version answer three times in one month. Who is responsible for fixing it, and what do they do first?"

A good answer names a source owner and a system owner who look at the pipeline together. They check which version was indexed and when, and whether a withdrawal reached the index. You may think the software vendor owns the problem. I ask: "Who at the firm approved that source when it went in?"

Now that we know what a sound system looks like, we try it on our own library in class.
06.17:
This is the in-class work, about thirty minutes, done together. I show the first example and you then direct the changed one. Step one is to open the manifest of the 40-document synthetic library and choose the current M-01 agreement. Step two is a connected search, only if one exists and I have rehearsed it in the real account. Otherwise I run the local script with the method you choose, say which method it is (lexical word matching, LSA, or hybrid), and mark any connected search that was not run.

Step three is to test the current version, a missing answer, the preserved exception and an access boundary, using the scoring sheet. Step four is to record the retrieved IDs and the answers separately and compare them with the reference. I never describe the prepared trace as a run.

Before we begin I ask: "Which document in the manifest is the current M-01 agreement, and how do you know?"

I am listening for CONTRACT-01 v2, status current, matter M-01.

Once we have results, the next slide states what we are entitled to conclude from them.
06.18:
We read the two conclusions on the slide. First, source selection and answer fidelity are separate tests. Choosing the current permitted source is mandatory. The language model then has to keep the exception and say which facts are missing. Second, the local scripts are demonstrations. Lexical is word matching. LSA is a classical vector method learned from the 40 documents only. Neither is a neural embedding model or a live RAG product. They show version and access filtering only. A neural embedding route exists in the files (embedding_selftest.py and Embedding Demo Run Sheet.txt) and has not been run yet, so we do not claim a result from it.

I ask you to give me the conclusion in your own words before I summarise. Then I ask: "Which part of today's result is still unverified?"

What I want to hear is that we have not tested neural embedding retrieval or a live RAG product, and that what we ran shows what happened in that run only. One run says nothing about how often it would happen. If you claim the class proved the product works, I ask: "What exactly did the local scripts demonstrate, and what did they leave untested?"

I keep any open questions in the record, and the next slide turns this into a decision for the firm.
06.19:
This is a class decision record. It carries no firm authorisation. The proposed decision is to pilot a maintained, permitted collection with an owner, independent test cases and update rules. I ask you to write down one owner and one condition before going on, and to list the evidence still needed.

I ask: "What result in the pilot would make you change this decision?"

A good answer names something checkable: a critical access failure, a repeated wrong-version answer, weak scores on answer fidelity, or a change in which matters the collection covers. You should say you would revisit the plan if the evidence, the quality or the permitted scope changes. If the answer is "if people don't like it", I ask: "What would you measure to know that?"

We finish with three questions that change the facts, and I ask them before I open the key.
06.20:
I ask these three questions before I show the answer key, and I let you work on each one.

First: "The answer uses the right version but invents an ownership fact. Which test fails?" A good answer is answer fidelity and uncertainty handling. The source choice was right, and the answer said more than the sources support.

Second: "Search finds no current permitted source. What should happen?" What I want to hear is that the assistant returns a gap or asks a clarifying question and does not invent an answer.

Third: "Could keyword retrieval be part of a RAG system?" Yes. RAG can use keyword, vector or hybrid retrieval, so vectors alone do not define it.

If the third answer is no, I ask: "What does RAG require, according to the definition on slide 5?"

That closes the main session. If we have time or you ask, the optional slides follow, starting with embeddings. Otherwise the next session covers legal research and deep research.
06.21:
I use this slide only if you ask what the vectors are. An embedding is a list of numbers that represents a piece of text, built so that a computer can compare two pieces for similarity. In our matter, the question and each candidate chunk can both be turned into such lists and compared.

LSA builds its vectors from the 40 documents alone, so it is a classical method, whereas a neural embedding model is trained elsewhere on much more text. In our scripts both can be compared once the neural one has been run on your own machine.

I ask: "Does making an embedding of a document mean we have retrained the model?"

A good answer is no. An existing embedding model computes the numbers, and nothing is retrained. A two-dimensional picture of these lists is a drawing that simplifies a much larger space, and it does not prove two clauses mean the same. You may think a high similarity score decides the legal answer. I ask: "What do you check after ranking, before you rely on the clause?"

I would then go to the next optional slide on how much to put in context.
06.22:
Not every task needs retrieval. If the question concerns a few documents we can choose ourselves, we put them directly into the model's context window, which is the amount of text the model can read in one go. For a larger collection that changes, we use retrieval with source, access and update controls. CAG, cache-augmented generation, preloads a manageable collection into context and reuses supported cached computation. The sources still need updating, since a cache does not refresh stale evidence.

I ask: "When would giving the model the two agreement versions directly be enough for the firm?"

What I want to hear is a small, permitted set of documents for a bounded question, such as comparing v1 and v2 for this one matter. If you think a bigger context window removes any need for access control, I ask: "Who may see every document in that window?"

The next optional slide shows what the assistant should do when the source gives no answer.
06.23:
Some questions cannot be answered from the sources. The current documents do not establish the ownership chain, and the signed Fee Schedule is missing, so the annual fees cannot be stated. The right response is an evidence gap and never an invented transaction detail.

I ask: "A partner asks, 'Does Victoria have to consent to Equator's reorganisation?' What is a useful response, given what we hold?"

A good answer states what the agreement says in the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6 (KT-1): consent is not required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group if Provider remains responsible, and then asks for the ownership chart, written confirmation of continued responsibility, and whether any assignment is planned. A citation next to a made-up fact still leaves the fact made up. If you offer a guess about fees, I ask: "Which document would contain that number?"

The last optional slide asks how the firm might buy this ability.
06.24:
This slide frames a purchasing choice. The firm can compare a feature in its existing document management system (DMS) with a separate retrieval service. We assess source control, access, integration and review effort. Building our own adds maintenance work that someone has to carry.

I ask: "A vendor says its product handles legal search. What should it demonstrate with our sample before we believe it?"

I am listening for these: correct retrieval of the current version, answers that link to sources, a clear response when the answer is missing, and respect for access boundaries. A vendor claim becomes evidence only after a test on our own documents and permissions. If you accept a demo built on the vendor's data, I ask: "What would change if we used our own matter files?"

That finishes the optional slides, and the next session moves to legal research and deep research.

07.1: Welcome to Session 7. Today we take one legal question to a short memo where every claim has a source and every limit is stated. The result is a claim-to-source register and an audited short research memo. We read a real public Ugandan judgment, and Victoria's own question stays separate from it. First, the recall question on the next slide.
07.2:
I ask the recall question before I say anything about the answer: "A retrieved passage has a valid citation. What remains before advice?" Last session the tool found passages in the firm's own files. Today the tool goes further and searches outside the firm, so the same habit matters more.

I am listening for three steps. Read the passage itself. Check that the authority is the right one and the right version. Then ask whether the passage supports the proposition we want, on our client's facts. If you only say "check the citation", I ask: "A citation can be real and still say something different from what the memo claims. Where would you look to find out?"

Today's question is on the right of the slide, and the result is the register and the audited memo. Now we turn the question into something we can actually research, which is the job of the next slide.
07.3:
A question is researchable when it has an issue, a jurisdiction, a relevant date, the facts, and a stated output. Today we hold two questions side by side. The historical question is how the Goal Relief court treated the programme delivery fee. The client question is what evidence and current law a proposed overseas support fee for Victoria would need.

The third line on the slide is the discipline: keep the court's facts and Victoria's unconfirmed facts apart. The court decided a dispute between other parties in other periods.

I ask: "Looking at the client question, which facts would you need from Victoria before any search is useful?" A good answer lists the supplier, the nature of the service, the payment date and the contract terms.

The next slide shows how we plan the research before any tool writes a report.
07.4:
A plan comes before a report. The four lines are the plan: the question and jurisdiction, the sources we will search and the ones we exclude, the subquestions and any conflicting positions, and the evidence that would support a conclusion.

I will use the word deep research a lot today. It means a tool that takes a question, makes its own plan of searches, reads what it finds, and writes a long report with references. It may revise its plan as it goes. Many tools show you that plan before they start. If your tool does that, this is your first checkpoint.

I ask: "The tool shows you its plan for the Victoria question. What do you check before you let it run?" What I want to hear is that you check the scope and whether the plan leaves out the decisive legal issue, such as the dates or the jurisdiction.

Plans depend on sources, so the next slide sorts sources by what each one can establish.
07.5:
This table is a way of asking, for each kind of source, what we must establish before we rely on it. It is a set of roles. It does not rank sources for every jurisdiction, and a qualified lawyer decides what binds and how later cases treated it.

For legislation we need the text, when it came into force, and any amendments. For a judgment we need the court, the issue, the reasoning and the disposition. For official guidance we need who issued it, the date, its scope and its status. Commentary explains and gives leads to primary authority, and we follow the lead to the original.

I ask: "A vendor's summary of a judgment looks tidy and has a link. Can it replace reading the judgment?" A good answer says no. We treat the summary as a lead and read the authority itself.

To practise that, the next slide gives us one real public authority to inspect.
07.6:
Here is the case we will read: Goal Relief Development Organisation v Uganda Revenue Authority, Civil Appeal 50 of 2023, [2024] UGCommC 272. It is a public judgment, and I use it as a research-reading exercise. We take the title, court and date from the judgment itself, and we do not copy them from a summary.

I keep a note of how we access it. The text we hold is a downloaded reproduction of the court's text. That is enough for reading the historical decision. It tells us nothing about current law or how later courts treated the case.

I ask: "This case is about tax. What would you check before applying it to Victoria?" I am listening for the issue, the material facts, the holding, the court, later treatment, and how well it fits our question.

Before we read it, the next slide shows how to use AI on a judgment without letting a summary change its meaning.
07.7:
These are four moves for reading a judgment, and an AI tool can help with each. Identify the parties and the procedural posture, meaning how the case reached this court. Find the issue and the court's reasoning. Separate what the parties submitted from what the court found. Check the order at the end.

When I ask a tool to summarise, I also ask for paragraph or page references, and then I open those pages. A summary is only as good as its attribution. Suppose the summary says "VAT was charged on the fee". It matters whether the court said that, or whether the appellant said it in argument.

I ask: "Where can a summary reverse the meaning of a judgment?" A good answer names attribution, procedural history, qualifications, or the final disposition.

The attribution point is the most common slip, so the next slide spends its time on submission and finding.
07.8:
This slide has two boxes. On the left, a party argues, and an argument in submissions only tells us that party's position. On the right, the court decides, and a finding or holding needs support in the court's own reasoning or in its order.

In Goal Relief I find a short passage in the judgment and read it with you, and we label who says it. If the judgment is not available on the day, I use the prepared fictional attribution exercise, say clearly that it is fictional, and I do not invent a holding for the real case.

I ask: "What must the memo label accurately for every proposition?" What I want to hear is who said it and what legal status it has: appellant's submission, respondent's submission, finding, or order.

Once the speaker is clear, the next slide asks which version of the law the court was applying.
07.9:
Law changes, so every legislative proposition needs a date. The four lines are: identify the enactment and provision, check amendments and commencement, match the version to the date of the question, and trace any quoted wording back to the source.

Three dates are easy to mix up. The publication date is when a text was published. The effective date is when it applied. The access date is when we looked at it. A current consolidated page may not answer a question about an earlier period.

I ask: "Suppose Victoria makes a payment to an overseas supplier in September 2026, a date I have made up for the exercise. Which date matters when we check the law, and why?" A good answer says the position at the relevant time for the transaction, established through the sources, and that we record the date we checked. If you say "the latest version", I ask: "What if the payment date falls before an amendment starts?"

The next slide shows why a section number is tied to an edition, using the judgment we have in front of us.
07.10:
Look at the first row. The Goal Relief judgment, at printed page 3, lines 24 to 27, cites section 27(2) of Cap 341, 7th Revised Edition, for the rule that an appeal to the High Court may be made on questions of law only. I read that line to you from the PDF.

A section number belongs to an edition of the statute. Acts are revised and consolidated, and the numbers can change between editions. A number copied from a judgment tells us what that court cited on that date. It does not tell us what the provision is called now.

I ask: "A summary gives you 'section 27(2)' for the appeal rule. What do you do before you put it in advice to Victoria?" A good answer says we open the current consolidated Act, find the provision, record its edition and the date we looked, and check whether the wording still says the same thing. If you say you would trust the judgment, I ask: "Which edition did the court cite, and which edition applies to our transaction?"

Now we move from reading authorities to a tool that searches for them, in the deep-research cycle.
07.11:
This slide builds in four clicks, and each click adds one stage of the cycle. The first click shows Plan: the tool frames subquestions. The second shows Search: it finds candidate authority. The third shows Inspect: it reads and compares what it found. The fourth shows Synthesize: it answers with limitations.

A tool can loop back. If inspecting a source raises a new question, it can plan and search again. Deep research is a product mode and a working pattern. It does not promise that the search was complete or the result correct. We stay in the loop and check scope and authority at each stage.

After the fourth click I ask: "What would make the cycle go round again?" I am listening for a missing authority, two conflicting propositions, or a doubt about whether the source is current.

Even a good cycle ends in a report, and the next slide explains why the report cannot be treated as the evidence.
07.12:
The report is a claim about the sources. The sources are the evidence. So we check each claim in four steps: open the cited source, find the passage that supports the claim, check that the passage says what the report says it does, and record gaps and any contrary authority.

I should define one word here. A hallucination is an output that reads confidently and is wrong, such as an invented case or a quotation that is not in the source. Retrieval and search tools reduce this risk and do not remove it. A working link also proves little, because it may lead to a real judgment that says something else, or to a passage that only records a party's submission.

I ask: "A citation in the report is genuine but does not support the claim. What do we do?" A good answer corrects or removes the claim and continues the research.

To practise that checking, the next slide gives us a note with a claim that no source supports.
07.13:
This is the practice slide. Open Flawed Research Note.txt in the Research and Review folder. It is a constructed exercise, written for checking, and it is not a model output. It claims our client is exempt from every filing because it is reorganising internally, and no supplied source establishes that.

You direct the work. I ask you to identify what would be needed to support the proposition, then we inspect the supplied authorities and set their facts beside Victoria's. We record what remains unresolved in the Evidence Register.

I ask: "What should the corrected note say?" What I want to hear is that the materials do not establish a blanket exemption, and that we must define the specific obligations and research each. If a research tool is unavailable, we work from the supplied sources only and mark any fresh search as unexecuted.

Next we look at what we are allowed to put into a search box, because research queries leave the firm.
07.14:
A search query is information leaving the firm. Even with no document uploaded, a query can reveal a matter. A public search engine, or a tool that is not approved by the firm, can expose a client's identity or plans.

The slide gives three habits. Use an approved tool. Use the minimum facts needed. Keep public-law research apart from confidential matter analysis. For example, I can search for the legal treatment of an overseas software support fee in Uganda without naming Victoria or the amount, then bring the answer back into the private file to apply it.

I ask: "If we remove the company name from a query, is the fact pattern anonymous?" A good answer is no, because a distinctive combination of facts, such as an unusual structure, a date and a sector, can still identify the client.

With the query kept safe, the next slide shows the shape of the memo that comes out of the research.
07.15:
A short memo has four parts. The question and the material facts. The applicable sources and the analysis. The uncertainty and the contrary points. Then the advice, or the next questions for review.

I generate a draft only after we have a few checked claims in the register. I keep quotations and analysis apart, so the reader sees which words belong to the court and which are ours. You and I then review it together.

Here is a concrete case. The historical holding goes in the sources and analysis section. Victoria's open questions go in the uncertainty section: the supplier, the service terms, the dates and current law.

I ask: "A tool gives a generic opening paragraph about VAT in Uganda. What would you remove?" I am listening for background that does not help answer the defined issue.

A memo can read well and still be weak, so the next slide gives us three tests of its quality.
07.16:
These three questions are the test of a research memo. Can a second lawyer reproduce the source trail? Does the memo distinguish facts, authority and inference? Would the conclusion change if a key source were withdrawn?

I ask you to choose the weakest claim in our draft and correct it where we can both see the correction. Visible corrections show that the process works. A hidden one teaches nothing.

I ask: "What does a useful uncertainty statement do?" A good answer names the missing evidence and says how it could affect the advice. For instance: "We have not confirmed the payment date, and if it falls before an amendment the answer may differ." If you offer "more research is needed", I ask: "Which source, and what would it change?"

We have all the pieces now, and the next slide sets out the work we do together in the class exercise.
07.17:
This is the in-class work, and we do it together. I run the first example on screen, and you then direct the changed one.

There are four steps. We read the court's reasoning and orders in Goal Relief, using the Ground 5 pages. We check the edition the judgment cites and then read the same provision in the current consolidated Act. We run a deep-research task if your account allows it, then check every material authority and proposition. Last, we audit the memo's claims, sources and the gaps that remain.

I save whatever the tools actually produce, and I record it in the Research Run Record.

I ask: "Using the public Goal Relief decision, how did the court treat the programme delivery fee, and which conclusion belongs to the court rather than a party?" If your account or the connected tool is unavailable, I use the saved judgment text, mark the fresh search as unexecuted, and keep the time for the explanation.

Now we compare what we found with the model result on the next slide.
07.18:
Before I show you the conclusion, I ask you to state your own. Then I compare it with this slide.

On Ground 5 the court held that Goal Ireland's fundraising for the appellant was a service imported by the appellant. So VAT on the 10% programme delivery fee was correctly assessed, and the court dismissed the appeal with costs, at printed pages 22 to 24. It is a historical result between other parties and does not decide Victoria's position.

The second point says the downloaded court-text reproduction supports the reading exercise, and that current law and later treatment need fresh research.

I ask: "Which part of today's result is still unverified?" What I want to hear is the paragraph, the statute edition, the client facts, and current law and later treatment.

The next slide turns this result into a decision for the firm.
07.19:
The decision on this slide is to adopt a claim-level research record, with an accountable reviewer and explicit unresolved questions. We record the decision and the evidence still needed. In class this is a decision record. It does not authorise anything for the firm.

I ask you to name an owner and one condition before the practice goes ahead. For example, the owner is the supervising partner, and the condition is that no memo leaves the firm until each material claim has a checked passage in the register.

I ask: "What evidence would change this proposed decision?" A good answer says we revisit it if the evidence, the quality of the work, or the permitted scope changes.

Then we test whether the ideas hold up when the facts change, in the check on the next slide.
07.20:
I ask these three questions before opening any answer key, one at a time, and I let you answer in your own words.

First: "A later summary contradicts the historical judgment. Which text must be inspected?" Second: "Section numbers differ between editions. What must the memo record?" Third: "Can the historical holding decide Victoria's proposed fee?"

What I want to hear is this. We inspect both actual authorities and the later treatment, and we do not choose between summaries. The memo records the Act, the edition and date, the provision and the proposition. The client's facts and the applicable current law need their own analysis, so the holding does not decide Victoria's fee.

If an answer is partial, I pick the missing part and ask again: "What does the memo need to say so that a reader can find the exact provision?"

That ends the main session. In Session 8 we turn from research to contract review and drafting, using the same evidence-first habit on an agreement.
07.21:
This optional slide lists five ways research goes wrong and the review response for each. An invented citation: verify that the authority exists. Wrong jurisdiction: check relevance and authority. An old provision: check dates and amendments. Selective support: search for contrary treatment. An overbroad conclusion: narrow it to what the evidence supports.

A research tool that uses retrieval can still produce a hallucination. I do not quote error percentages from old studies as the performance of any tool you use today.

I ask: "What should the firm measure on its own matters?" A good answer says task accuracy, completeness, whether the source supports the claim, and the time spent on review.

I use this slide only if you have a question or we agreed extra time. Otherwise we close with the essential conclusion from slide 18.
07.22:
This optional slide connects the session to how the firm works. Three things make research an organisational capability: shared source registers and maintained precedents, a review standard for AI-assisted advice, and a route for correcting and sharing findings.

The idea is that checked research is kept with its dates and restrictions, so the firm does not collect unverified chatbot outputs.

I ask: "Who maintains reusable advice in your firm?" A good answer names a practice or knowledge owner working under the firm's review arrangements. If you say "everyone", I ask: "When two partners disagree about a finding, who decides and where is it recorded?"

I use this slide only if time allows, and it is the last slide of the session.

08.1: Welcome to Session 8. Today we use an AI model, which is a program that has learned patterns from large amounts of text and writes the most likely next words, to help review a contract and draft a change to it. The question on the slide is how this support can sit alongside your own legal judgement. We finish with a repaired three-finding review and one amendment you can defend. Everything runs on the fictional Victoria and Equator matter.
08.2:
I begin with last session before showing anything. I ask: a party argues that a fee is not taxable, and our memo wants to say "the court found" that. May the memo label that as the court's finding?

I am listening for a no, with the reason that a party's submission is an argument, and the finding and the order come from the court's own reasoning and disposition. If the answer is partial, I ask: which part of the judgment would you quote to show what the court actually decided?

Then I read today's question on the slide and the result we are aiming for, so you know the research habit of tracing each statement to its source carries straight into contract work.

Now that research discipline is fresh, the next slide sets out the contract-review brief we will work on today.
08.3:
Here is the matter in three lines. Equator Systems Ltd, the Provider, proposes a group reorganisation. We act for Victoria Services Ltd, the Customer, so every view we take is customer-side. The partner has asked for a review against the firm playbook, and the review must keep qualifications and missing facts visible.

I ask: before we touch any tool, what would make a result from this review acceptable to the partner?

What I want to hear is that each statement is taken accurately from the agreement, is compared with the relevant playbook point, and that anything we do not know is written down as unknown. Victoria has not sent us the ownership chart or written confirmation that Equator remains responsible. If you leave those gaps out, I ask: what would the partner assume if the review stayed silent about them?

Next, the slide on the current agreement tells us which document we are working from and what status each version has.
08.4:
Three documents can get mixed up, so I fix their status now. CONTRACT-01 v2 is the executed teaching agreement. Draft v1 is still in the folder and is labelled as superseded, so we never quote from it. Any redline we produce is a new draft for review and has no effect on the signed agreement.

I ask: when we propose a change to Section 12.6, what must the proposal carry with it?

A good answer says the source section, the proposed wording, and the reason for the change. Anyone who picks up the draft should be able to see which signed text it responds to.

The misconception I watch for is that a generated change somehow amends the contract. If I hear that, I ask: who would have to sign for Section 12.6 to change?

Now that the status of each document is settled, the next slide shows how a tool picks names out of the agreement.
08.5:
Named entity recognition, or NER, is the task of finding names and labelling them by type. On the slide, the tool finds Victoria Services Ltd and Equator Systems Ltd and labels each an organisation, and it finds 15 August 2026 and labels it a date. These labels describe the kind of thing the words are. They do not say what either company must do.

I ask: the tool has extracted "Equator Systems Ltd" as an organisation. Has it established that Equator owes any particular obligation?

I am listening for a no. The label says organisation. To learn that Equator is the Provider and must obtain Victoria's consent in some circumstances, we have to read the surrounding text of Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms.

If you say yes, I ask: which words in the agreement tell us what Equator must do?

The next slide shows what a complete record of one obligation looks like once a name has been found.
08.6:
An obligation record has four parts. First, the actor and the action required. Second, the trigger or timing. Third, the conditions and exceptions. Fourth, the exact source and a review status, such as checked or not checked.

Take the sentence in Section 12.6 (the Key Terms replacement, KT-1) that Provider must obtain Customer's prior written consent before a change of control of Provider takes effect. The actor is Equator, the action is obtaining Victoria's written consent, and the timing is before the change takes effect. The exception sits in the next sentence.

I ask: if a field is empty, how do we know whether the source says nothing or the tool simply failed to find it?

A good answer says we go back to the exact passage and read it ourselves, then record which of the two it is.

The next slide takes Section 12.6 apart so we can see the rule, its exception and its condition one at a time.
08.7:
This slide has three clicks, and I read the real wording of Section 12.6 from the agreement before the first one. The operative rule is the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6 (KT-1), which controls over the Standard Terms. The unmodified Standard Terms version, which lets either party assign on notice after a merger, change of control, reorganization or sale, is overridden.

The first click shows the rule: Provider must obtain Customer's prior written consent before a change of control of Provider takes effect. The second shows the exception: that consent is not required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group. The third shows the condition on the exception: if Provider remains responsible for its obligations under this Agreement.

I ask: if a tool extracted only the first sentence about consent, what would the review get wrong?

A good answer says it would overstate the consent requirement, because the group exception and its condition would vanish. A follow-up if needed: on our facts, has anyone shown that Equator is wholly owned within a group or that it stays responsible?

Next, the playbook slide compares these terms with what the firm prefers for a customer.
08.8:
The table sets the source position beside the playbook preference. The source gives prior consent with an exception, and the playbook prefers a clear change-of-control boundary. The group exception depends on Provider remaining responsible, and the playbook is willing to keep a workable exception. Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms has no separate notice step for an internal reorganisation, and the playbook says to consider adding one.

Remember that the playbook is a fictional set of firm preferences. It is a measure of what we would like for the customer and says nothing about what the law requires.

I ask: if a clause departs from the playbook, does that make the clause unlawful?

What I want to hear is no: a departure may be a commercial or drafting preference, and calling it unlawful needs a legal source. If the answer is partial, I ask: what would we cite to support a claim that a term is unlawful?

Now we test a review against the source, and the next slide gives you one with mistakes in it.
08.9:
I give you a review that contains three findings, and you check each against the executed agreement. Finding one says every reorganisation needs consent. Finding two says support staff need no customer approval. Finding three says the agreement fixes fees at UGX 50 million.

I open the agreement for each finding. Section 12.6, as replaced by the Key Terms, has the group exception, so the first finding leaves it out. Section 1.5, as supplemented by the Key Terms, lets Provider give support staff access only if each person is named in a written request and Customer has approved that person in writing first. The signed Fee Schedule is not supplied, so no figure can be stated.

I ask: which passage lets you correct each finding, and what do you write for the fee?

A good answer gives the three corrections and writes that the fee is unknown until we receive the signed schedule. If it is a run of the tool, I save the actual output.

Next, the review table puts each repaired finding into a form another partner can check.
08.10:
This table is the repaired review. Each row names the source, states the finding, and gives the next step. Section 12.6 shows an exception with conditions, and we confirm ownership and responsibility. Section 1.5 shows prior approval for support access, and we check the named people and the approval. The fee row says the Fee Schedule is absent, and we obtain the signed schedule.

The footer matters: partner approval decides how a finding is used.

I ask: what would let another partner check this review in a few minutes?

I am listening for exact passages, clear labels for each issue, and a visible reason for each next step. Ownership facts that we do not have sit in their own place, away from the wording of the agreement. If you offer only a neat layout, I ask: where would the reader find the exact words of Section 1.5?

With a checked review in hand, the next slide turns to drafting and what must go in before any model writes a word.
08.11:
There are four clicks. The first shows Instructions, meaning the client objective: for example, Victoria wants to know about an internal reorganisation. The second shows Sources, the agreement and any precedent we supply. The third shows Draft, the proposed wording the model produces. The fourth shows Review, where a lawyer checks meaning and consequences.

Everything the model works from has to fit in its context window, which is the amount of text it can take in at once. That is why we choose what to put in.

I ask: if the model needs a fact we have not given it, such as the new owner of Equator, what should it do?

A good answer says it should ask or mark an assumption in the draft, and should never fill the gap quietly. A tool may hallucinate, which means it states something that sounds right but has no support. If the answer is partial, I ask: how would you spot an invented fact in a draft?

Next, the slide shows a current clause beside a drafted addition.
08.12:
The left side states the current position: the wholly owned group-reorganisation exception applies if the provider remains responsible. The right side is a draft for discussion: add a notice requirement for a qualifying internal reorganisation, with timing and recipient to agree.

This is a drafting option that fits the firm's customer-side playbook. Nothing says the law requires a notice term.

I ask: if we proposed this notice, which details would still need to be agreed?

I am listening for the notice period, who receives it, the evidence that goes with it, and what happens if Equator fails to give it. Victoria's Notice Address is in the Order Form, so recipient is a fair place to start. If those points are missing, I ask: what would Equator ask us to give in return?

If a tool is available, I run the first version live and keep the real output. If not, I use a labelled example and mark it unexecuted.

The next slide asks what each proposed change must carry to be a usable redline.
08.13:
A redline shows the changes between two versions, and each one needs a reason. I go through the four points on the slide. Link each change to the client objective. Keep defined terms and cross-references intact. Check how the change interacts with other clauses. Record the partner's decision to accept or reject.

An example: our added notice must fit with Section 12.9, part of the unmodified Standard Terms, which says notices must be in writing and sent to the Notice Address. If our wording says something different about delivery, the two clauses collide.

I ask: a model suggests a smoother wording of a sentence in Section 12.6. Does better grammar justify the change?

What I want to hear is that it does not, until we have checked the effect on legal meaning and on the commercial position. If the answer is partial, I ask: which word in that sentence could change who has to consent?

Next, we turn to the style of the draft itself and how to catch writing that sounds generic.
08.14:
Drafts from a model often read the same way: warm opening, general praise, and legal-sounding phrases with little content. The slide gives three fixes. Remove generic praise and unnecessary legal-sounding language. Use the firm's voice and defined terms, such as Provider and Customer. Keep each sentence tied to the real issue.

I put a generic paragraph beside a precise one on the group exception. The precise one says Victoria's consent is not required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group if Provider remains responsible for its obligations.

I ask: when you shorten a sentence, which words must stay even if the sentence gets longer?

A good answer says the conditions that affect legal meaning, in this case the wholly owned group and Provider remaining responsible. A follow-up: if we cut the second condition, who gains?

Next, the responsibilities slide sets out who owns each stage once the draft exists.
08.15:
The table assigns an owner and a record to each stage. Extraction belongs to the operator or tool and leaves a source-linked draft. Legal interpretation belongs to a qualified reviewer and leaves a checked finding. Client advice belongs to an authorised partner and leaves an approved version. Retention belongs to the matter owner and leaves the final record with its source trail.

Using AI for a stage leaves the professional accountability where it was. The software has no standing to advise Victoria.

I ask: who in our firm may approve the advice that goes to Victoria, and what do they need to see first?

I am listening for the person authorised under the firm's professional and internal arrangements, and for the checked finding with its sources. I would also name the actual people at this point. If you say the reviewer, I ask: does the reviewer's check amount to approval to advise the client?

Now we move into our own work, and the next slide lists what we do together.
08.16:
This is the practice block, and we do it together in class. I demonstrate the first step and keep the actual output. You predict the answer, choose the evidence, and check the changed example.

Step one: extract parties, roles and obligations, checking definitions and cross-references. Step two: repair the three flawed findings. Step three: apply Variant B, where Equator proposes to assign the agreement. The first sentence of Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms requires Victoria's prior written consent to any assignment, and an assignment without it is void. The group exception sits with change of control and does not excuse consent to an assignment. Step four: draft one customer-side amendment with a reason and mark it for qualified review.

I ask before step three: does the change-of-control sentence answer the assignment question?

If the tool is unavailable, I use a labelled example, mark the step unexecuted, and use the time for explanation. Any saved run shows what happened once.

The next slide gathers what we can conclude from this work.
08.17:
Before I summarise, I ask you to say the conclusion in your own words. Then I compare it with the slide.

The first point: NER finds names and leaves out most legal relationships. The three errors lost the exception, reversed the support approval and invented a fee. Assignment is not settled by the change-of-control sentence alone. The second point: the agreement is fictional teaching material built on a public template. It is not a production contract or legal opinion.

I ask: which part of today's result remains unverified?

A good answer says the facts we lack, such as ownership and Equator's continued responsibility, and any outputs we did not run. It also says that what we produced is a classroom exercise and a real matter would need the real documents and a qualified review. If you name only one gap, I ask: what else would we request from Victoria?

Next, the decision slide records what the firm will do with these results.
08.18:
We record one decision: maintain a customer-side playbook and require a reason and source for each proposed change. I write down an owner and one condition under which we go ahead.

I ask: what evidence would change this decision?

A good answer is that we revisit it if the evidence, the quality of the output, or the permitted scope changes. This is a class decision record and carries no firm authorisation.

Then I move to the check-understanding questions.
08.19:
I ask three changed-fact questions before opening the answer key. First, Equator proposes assigning the agreement: does the change-of-control sentence in Section 12.6 (Key Terms version) settle permission? Second, the company name is extracted: has its obligation been established? Third, the signed schedule is absent: may our amendment assume a fee?

The answers I want are these. On assignment, the first sentence of Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms asks for Victoria's prior written consent, and the group exception speaks to change of control. On the name, a label establishes no obligation, so we need the surrounding text. On the fee, no, we ask for the signed schedule. In one saved Variant B run, a model reached the consent answer, and that shows one result only.

If the answers are partial, I ask: which passage supports that?

That closes Session 8. In Session 9 we look at automation and agentic AI, and who controls what a tool may do.
08.20:
This optional slide separates three tasks. Entity recognition asks what named item appears, for example Equator Systems Ltd. Relationship extraction asks who is linked to what, for example Provider under this agreement. Obligation extraction asks who must do what and when, for example Customer consent before a change of control.

I ask: what could a flat list of entities miss?

A good answer says it misses who owes the duty and when the exception applies. If you stall, I ask: which of the three rows would tell us that Equator needs Victoria's consent?

I use this slide only if you ask, and then return to the session conclusion.
08.21:
This optional slide separates summary from issue spotting. A summary describes what the clause says. Issue spotting compares the clause with the task, the facts and the playbook, and names a reason to review.
