If you suggest training the staff to review faster, I ask: what would faster review do to the accuracy of the finding?

This shows how fragile a gain can be, so the next slide turns to the route for obtaining the capability in the first place.
12.10:
There are three routes in the table. We can buy an existing product, configure a platform, or commission custom development. The right-hand column tells the partner what to assess on each. For a product, that is task fit, sources, rights and contract. For a platform, connections, permissions and support. For custom development, ownership, evaluation and maintenance.

An agent is software that takes steps toward a goal using a model, such as searching and then drafting. A custom agent is not automatically more capable or cheaper. It also needs someone to maintain it.

Here is the step I would take with any vendor. I give them a sample of our permitted documents and ask them to work on it.

I ask: what should we request from a vendor beyond a polished demo? I am listening for tests we can repeat, a list of failures, the review effort, the operating cost and the arrangements for leaving.

If you mention only price, I ask: what happens to our work if the vendor closes?

Whichever route we take, someone must run the pilot, so the next slide names the pilot team.
12.11:
I read the four roles. A sponsor with decision authority. Practice and information owners. Technical support and qualified reviewers. And the staff who will use the process. In a small firm one person may hold two of these roles. The goal is clear responsibilities, and a new committee is not needed.

Take a concrete case. The tax team's precedent library changes when a new ruling is added. Somebody has to update it and say when it was last checked.

I ask: who owns the freshness of the sources? What I want to hear is the named information or knowledge owner.

If you say the vendor or the tool, I ask: who in this firm can say what the current version of that source is?

I also ask who can say no. If you say the sponsor, that is a good answer, provided the sponsor really has the authority.

Now that we know who sits on the team, the next slide looks at how the rest of the staff come to use the process.
12.12:
We are at the guided application block now, and this slide is about the people. I read the four points. Explain which work changes and why. Demonstrate permitted uses with real workflow examples. Train reviewers as well as users. Provide an accessible feedback and incident route.

Adoption touches supervision and junior learning. A junior who never drafts a first research note may not learn how to judge one. The firm should decide how staff keep their domain skills and learn to challenge output.

I ask: what would make a lawyer avoid the approved process and go back to a private tool? I am listening for poor fit with the work, difficult access, unclear expectations or no one to ask.

If you say staff are simply resistant, I ask: what would you change in the process to make the approved route easier than the private one?

I ask you which of the four points you would write into your own proposal first.

People adopt a process when they trust how it treats clients, so the next slide takes up efficiency and service redesign.
12.13:
This slide concerns what the firm does with any time the process releases. I read the three points. Decide how quality and turnaround benefit clients. Review engagement terms and communication where relevant. Consider fees, value and accountability under applicable duties.

I say plainly that I am not giving a legal opinion on fees or disclosure. Those duties come from the firm's professional and contractual requirements, and the partners apply them.

A practical example. If research takes less time on a matter billed at a fixed fee, the client may expect a faster turnaround. If it is billed by time, the engagement terms matter. I do not assume released time turns into revenue.

I ask: who decides the pricing or disclosure position for work done with AI help? A good answer says the responsible partners, using the applicable professional and contractual requirements.

If you answer that the technology team decides, I ask: whose name is on the advice and the invoice?

After this decision about value, the next slide gives the stages by which the firm moves toward live use.
12.14:
Four clicks build this route. The first reveals Prepare, which means sources, scope and an owner. The second adds Shadow, where the assisted process runs next to the manual work and we compare the two. The third adds Pilot, which is bounded and authorised use. The fourth adds Review, where we expand, revise or stop.

The stages depend on evidence and agreed dates. They are not a promise of deployment in thirty days. I say that clearly because the 90-day plan on the next slide could be read as a launch schedule.

During Shadow, for example, a reviewer completes the same ten tasks by hand and with assistance and records the differences.

I ask: what evidence would let the firm expand after the Pilot stage? What I want to hear is quality results, access working as intended, operating performance and user adoption, all under the wider scope being proposed.

If you say the demo went well, I ask: what did the demo leave out?

With the stages clear, the next slide places them on a 90-day plan with owners.
12.15:
This table is a discussion plan, and it uses relative dates because no kickoff date or firm owner has been agreed. I read the rows. Days 0 to 30: practice and information owners settle scope, sources and baseline, and decide whether we are ready to shadow. Days 31 to 60: the workflow owner and reviewers run quality, effort and access tests and decide whether bounded use is justified. Days 61 to 90: the sponsor and risk owner weigh value and remaining risk and choose to expand, revise or stop.

Day 90 is a decision point. It is not an automatic expansion.

With you, we turn these into real names. Agree actual dates only if you are ready.

I ask: if data preparation takes longer than planned, what would you do? A good answer revises the plan and the scope, and keeps the source and access work in place.

If you say to start anyway, I ask: what would the shadow stage compare against?

The plan gives us the schedule, so the next slide lists what a partner-ready proposal must contain.
12.16:
This slide lists the four parts of the proposal we write together. The problem and selected workflow. The information, system and review design. The evidence and acceptance conditions. The ownership, resources and staged decision.

I have the Worked Pilot Proposal open and read it through once. Then we fill our own Pilot Proposal using decisions you have already made in the course. You should be able to explain every line without technical buzzwords.

An acceptance condition is a test result we agree beforehand, such as a stated share of cited findings that a reviewer confirms from the source.

I ask: what would another partner need to see in this proposal before they approve it? What I am listening for is a bounded purpose, the resources, named responsibilities, an evidence plan and a decision about the risk.

If you answer that the proposal needs more detail on the technology, I ask: which of the four parts is the weakest in what we have so far?

Next, the slide called Our in-class work sets out the order in which we build this.
12.17:
This is the working slide. Four tasks, done together. I set the time with you: the guide gives about thirty-five minutes for this block. First, repeat the diagnostic with changed examples. I do not show the model answers. Second, adapt the worked proposal to one candidate task: problem and baseline, scope and exclusions, sources and permissions, acceptance tests, owners. Third, check cost, review effort and the stress case from the Cost and Effort Example sheet. Fourth, assign proposed owners and relative day-30, 60 and 90 decisions.

I demonstrate the first example and you do the rest. We use files on your screen and the sheet, so no account or connected tool is needed. If a tool is unavailable, we use the labelled example and I mark that step unexecuted.

Before we begin, I ask you to state the exit diagnostic answer from the beginning, using the alternate facts. A good answer names a bounded problem, representative evidence, acceptance tests, resources, owners and a review decision.

When the work is done, the next slide states what we can conclude from it.
12.18:
I ask you to say the conclusion in your own words before I read the slide. Then we compare. The first point says a pilot needs a bounded problem, representative evidence, acceptance tests, resources, owners and a review decision. Time released is not automatically cash saved. The firm should state what evidence would justify expansion or stopping.

I connect this to the cost sheet. In the main case the monthly effect is a gain of UGX 160,000, valued at the cost of reviewer time. It becomes cash only if the freed capacity is used for paid work or avoids a real cost. In the stress case it is a loss of UGX 360,000.

I ask: which part of today's result remains unverified? A good answer says that a classroom proposal is not production approval, and that proposed roles and dates still need the firm's agreement.

If you think everything is settled, I ask: who has agreed to these dates?

Having stated what we know and what we do not, we move to the firm decision.
12.19:
This is the decision record. I say what it is: a class decision record. It is not authorisation by the firm. We write the recommendation as the slide says: prepare one proposal for firm review, with conditions and a next decision date. We name a proposed owner and one condition, and we list the evidence still needed.

For example, the condition could be that the information owner confirms the sources are permitted for this use before the shadow stage begins.

I ask: what evidence would change this proposed decision? I am listening for new results on quality, a change in the review effort, or a change in the permitted scope. If any of these moves, we revisit the proposal.

If you name only a cost change, I ask: what would you do if the reviewers found a critical error in the shadow stage?

When the record is written, I test your thinking with a short check using changed facts.
12.20:
These are three transfer questions. I read each one aloud and you answer before I open the key. I do not coach you.

The first: the draft saves time but loses a critical exception. Should we expand? The second: review effort rises above the manual baseline. What changes? The third: who can approve more users or action authority?

I am listening for these answers. Do not expand with a critical failure. Revise the design or stop if total effort or value is worse than the baseline. The named authorities in the firm decide scope and permissions, after further tests.

If your first answer is partial, I use a follow-up that fits it. On the first question I ask: how would a missed exception reach a client? On the second I ask: which number from the cost sheet changes first? On the third I ask: who in the firm holds that authority today?

Afterwards we compare your answers with the entry diagnostic. The next slides are optional, and I use them only if a question calls for them.
12.21:
This slide is optional. I use it if you ask why a good personal experiment is not yet a firm capability. On the left, an individual experiment: a person obtains a useful response from a familiar tool. On the right, a firm capability: colleagues can repeat the work using approved sources, review standards and an owned service.

I tell you the experiment has value. It is evidence, and it often points to the candidate pilot.

I ask: what must still be in place if the original user is away for a month? What I want to hear is usable instructions, sources, a review responsibility and operational support.

If you say the prompt is enough, I ask: who would update the sources the prompt depends on?

Since the personal experiment leads to a candidate pilot, the next optional slide returns to the first candidate.
12.22:
This slide is optional. It lists three candidate pilots: internal precedent and clause search, contract review against a maintained playbook, and tax evidence and reconciliation assistance. We choose one primary scope. The course has shown how the mechanisms connect. It has not shown that all three are ready for production.

For each candidate, I ask you what a qualified person could check. Searching for a precedent can be checked by opening the source. A review against a playbook depends on whether the playbook is maintained.

I ask: which of these has the clearest first quality test? I am listening for the one with accessible evidence and a result a qualified person can check.

If you pick the most ambitious one, I ask: what would the first test look like in week two?

The following optional slide covers what happens to a pilot once it is live.
12.23:
This optional slide lists three changes after launch. The provider updates the model. A source is amended or access changes. The process gains a new action or user group.

Each change can make earlier test results out of date. I give a concrete case. The vendor releases a new model version. The answers on our test set may now differ, so we retest before staff rely on it.

I say that the firm decides in advance what triggers retesting, approval and fresh instructions for staff.

I ask: what should happen before the process is given authority to file returns live? What I am listening for is a separate decision on authority, integration, risk and evaluation.

If you say to switch it on and watch, I ask: who would see a wrong filing before it reaches the regulator?

The last optional slide looks at what further study could add.
12.24:
This is the final optional slide. It lists four areas of further technical study: programming and model development, neural-network mathematics and optimisation, advanced retrieval and evaluation engineering, and production integration and security engineering.

A neural network is the layered mathematical structure inside most current models. I mention it so the term is clear.

The course gives you conceptual understanding and a route to implementation. It does not make you an independent production engineer, and I say so.

I ask: which of these areas would help the pilot we have chosen? A good answer picks the area by the real capability gap in the pilot and not by the vocabulary.

If you cannot choose, I ask: where did our proposal depend on someone else's skill?

This closes the session, and we keep the proposal and the decision record for the firm's review.
